title: Bonding & building - what we learned about Alonso's Chelsea in pre-season
summary: Chelsea's pre-season campaign was all about new manager Xabi Alonso, so what have we learned about his side?
full_text:
Bonding & building - what we learned about Alonso's Chelsea in pre-season
- Published
Chelsea's pre-season campaign was all about new manager Xabi Alonso but, in truth, the 56 hours spent travelling 24,561 miles by plane had been organised long before his appointment in May.
The Blues travelled further and longer than any other Premier League club, almost twice as much as during last season's US tour under former boss Enzo Maresca, visiting Sydney, Hong Kong and Jakarta before finishing in Iskandar Puteri, Malaysia, on Sunday.
It was tiring for many, not least Alonso, but that did not stop him setting standards by running off the jetlag at a remarkable pace of four minutes 30 seconds per kilometre alongside members of the club staff.
It set the tone for a culture of not making excuses, as did his involvement in a staff match before the squad flew out.
The 44-year-old former Spain World Cup winner was on the winning side and set up most of the goals.
Having already completed a substantial amount of fitness work for his players at home, including gruelling double sessions at the club's Cobham training base in the weeks leading up to the tour, Chelsea used the trip to focus on key tactical elements despite the demands of travel and fatigue.
- Como sign defender Chalobah from Chelsea 
  - Published2 hours ago
Hands-on approach and one-to-one sessions
Chelsea had done plenty of work to mitigate those demands. As well as hiring a private Airbus A340, the club immediately switched players on to Sydney time and instructed them to sleep after meals during the journey, which included a stop at Bandaranaike International Airport in Katunayake, Sri Lanka, before landing in Australia.
Training at Sky Park, home of Sydney FC, they had access to a compact but high-quality training facility, in addition to an open session at Allianz Stadium that was relatively low in intensity.
The session nevertheless offered an insight into Alonso's hands-on approach. He regularly demonstrated his passing ability, while testing players such as Estevao Willian by encouraging him to cross on his weaker right foot for team-mates to finish.
Alonso also smashed a 25-yard half-volley into the net at the end of the same session - a reminder of the qualities that made him one of the game's best midfielders during spells at Liverpool, Real Madrid and Bayern Munich.
England defender Levi Colwill confessed he was "jealous" of how well Alonso could "spray balls around".
"The manager was a great player, one of the best of his generation," added midfielder Romeo Lavia. "You see that when he steps into a training session.
"He starts pinging balls around in a way only those who have played at the top level can. It's a privilege to be working with him, especially as a midfielder."
Australia's rugby union head coach, and Chelsea supporter, Les Kiss visited after making the short walk from his team's headquarters and exchanged shirts with Alonso.
There were a number of 16 and 17-year-olds in the group, notably Sydney-born Mahdi Nicoll-Jazuli, who emerged as one of the tour's breakout performers with a series of impressive midfield displays.
He also attracted considerable interest from the Australian media, given his mother's links to the city and the prospect of representing the national team in the future, despite playing for England Under-17s.
Younger players were given time off to visit the cinema, go on boat trips and take in the local culture. There was table tennis, darts and computer games available at the team's luxury hotel, which overlooked Darling Harbour.
It was a quieter part of the trip when Chelsea and Tottenham players, who they faced in front of 80,000 fans on Saturday, were given the freedom to explore.
There were organised sponsor events near Bondi Beach, while another activity was a group visit to North Sydney Pool beneath the Harbour Bridge, where players completed a gym session before being allowed to enjoy the spa and Olympic-sized swimming pool. Goalkeeper Robert Sanchez also appeared on breakfast TV before the match.
Colwill described it as a fantastic team-bonding trip, although the 6-4 win over Western Sydney Wanderers and 2-1 defeat by Tottenham suggested it was still early days in terms of what Alonso was building.
Insiders said it initially felt similar to Mauricio Pochettino's regime, with a heavy focus on fitness, but tactical ideas were introduced as senior players returned from international duty.
In the first three matches, Alonso changed little about the 4-2-3-1 approach favoured by Maresca and later used during Liam Rosenior's short-lived spell in charge.
Key executives including co-owner Behdad Eghbali and sporting directors Paul Winstanley and Joe Shields were in Australia. It was clear transfer business continued between time zones as Chelsea worked on deals for Maxence Lacroix, Danny Welbeck, Jordan Henderson and later Spanish defender Pep Chavarria.
Alonso was also seen taking late arrivals Moises Caicedo and Nicolas Jackson aside for one-to-one sessions after their arrival from World Cup duty, physically testing them as they received passes from the coaching staff.
Australia was also the setting for Cole Palmer's first-ever pre-match media conference. He was relaxed, smiling and telling stories and, in his own blunt way, came across as charismatic.
Alonso was impressed by Palmer's fitness and hunger on his return and described him as a "leader", something reflected in his interaction with the younger players on tour.
Superstar treatment and set-pieces
Following another 10-hour private flight to Hong Kong, the squad stayed at the Kerry Hotel, where local fans regularly gathered in the hope of securing selfies and autographs.
Although the attention remained positive, the level of excitement required heightened security, with some supporters even booking rooms in the same hotel in the hope of encountering players in lifts and public areas.
Palmer and Colwill were given the freedom to go shopping after picking up knocks against Spurs, but videos of their outing showed just how well-known they were.
They were chased for selfies inside a local mall to highlight how big some of these Premier League stars are in Asia, while many players were presented with hand-crafted gifts to take home from those lucky enough to get close to their heroes.
It was in Hong Kong that Mykhailo Mudryk, along with Welbeck, Mike Penders, Geovany Quenda and Gabriel Slonina, joined up with the group.
Mudryk's arrival had not been planned, but Chelsea opted to treat him as a fully fledged member of the squad despite his 20-month absence after testing positive for the banned substance meldonium.
The reception was emotional throughout the Ukrainian forward's return. He received a hero's welcome during an open training session and later made his comeback as a substitute against Juventus last Wednesday, before a late assist in the 3-3 draw with Johor Darul Ta'zim.
Perhaps more significant from a pre-season perspective was the arrival of new set-piece coach Austin MacPhee, who immediately assumed a prominent role within training sessions.
With a notepad in hand and junior coaches acting as blockers, the Scot - who had a successful spell at Aston Villa - barked instructions throughout sessions.
It marked a stage of the tour during which tactical work increased significantly as Alonso's attacking patterns became more visible.
Those ideas were evident despite the 1-0 defeat by Juventus at the world-class Kai Tak Stadium, although a poor pitch made life difficult for both teams in attack.
Alonso and a few of his players and staff also played a round of golf on Thursday, others were out for meals, playing a virtual reality game and some went to see the famous Tian Tan Buddha on a scheduled day off.
"We have learned a lot in these two weeks, not just on the football side but on the personal side in getting to know each other," Alonso said.

title: Sunrisers thump Fire to close in on qualification
summary: Sunrisers Leeds move closer to securing qualification for The Hundred's knockout stages with a 71-run win over Welsh Fire, while a 101-run partnership helps London Spirit beat Birmingham Phoenix by seven wickets.
full_text:
Sunrisers thump Fire to close in on qualification
- Published
The Hundred men's competition, Headingley
Sunrisers Leeds 201-4 (100 balls): Marsh 50 (34); Woakes 2-41
Welsh Fire 130-6 (100 balls): Short 43 (29); Carse 3-24
Sunrisers Leeds won by 71 runs
Sunrisers Leeds moved closer to securing qualification for The Hundred's knockout stages with a comprehensive 71-run win over Welsh Fire.
Mitch Marsh, the tournament's leading run-scorer, struck his fourth half-century of the season for second-placed Sunrisers as they made 201-4 at Headingley.
The Australian opener hit a 34-ball 50 and added 89 for the first wicket with Ryan Rickelton.
Chris Woakes, who took 2-41, claimed the breakthrough when he had Rickelton caught for 40, while Harry Brook (23 from 11 balls) and Marsh fell within the space of five deliveries, caught off Jordan Clark and Lockie Ferguson respectively.
Captain Zak Crawley struck four sixes in a 12-ball 34 as Sunrisers pressed on, while Dan Lawrence (29) and Matthew Revis (15) ended the innings with an unbroken partnership of 27.
Fifth-placed Fire were unable to keep up with the required run-rate in their reply as only Matt Short (43) and Joe Root (31), who put on 49 for the second wicket, made more than 13.
Short was one of three victims for Brydon Carse, who also removed opener Phil Salt (13) and Marco Jansen (1).
Root was caught behind off Nathan Ellis, who also bowled Rachin Ravindra for two, while Jordan Cox also fell cheaply, caught for 12 off Matthew Potts.
Tom Kohler-Cadmore and Woakes both finished unbeaten on 13 as Fire closed on 130-6, well short of their target having chosen to chase at the toss.
Sunrisers now only need to avoid defeat against Manchester Super Giants on Tuesday to progress, while victory would put them in contention for top spot should leaders Trent Rockets lose against Southern Brave on Monday.
Fire, who would have moved second with a win on Sunday, are the lowest placed of three teams on 16 points and will likely need success against London Spirit on Wednesday and then rely on net run-rate to secure the final knockout spot.
- Who am I? Guess The Hundred cricket star No 20 
  - Published13 hours ago
Livingstone & Brevis shine as Spirit beat Phoenix
The Hundred men's competition, Headingley
Birmingham Phoenix 162-4 (100 balls): Clarke 73 (42), Dickson 51 (28); Crocombe 1-8
London Spirit 166-3 (82 balls): Livingstone 66 (30), Brevis 55 (31); Thompson 1-24
London Spirit won by seven wickets
Dewald Brevis and Liam Livingstone shared a 103-run partnership as London Spirit beat Birmingham Phoenix by seven wickets at Lord's.
In a match between two eliminated sides, Livingstone hit 66 from 30 balls, while Brevis struck an unbeaten 55 from 31 as Spirit passed their target of 163 with 18 balls to spare.
Coming together at 43-2 after the hosts had lost Jonny Bairstow and Lhuan-dre Pretorius for 10 and 16 respectively, the pair struck a collective total of 12 fours and seven sixes, hitting the ball deep into the stands on multiple occasions.
Home captain Livingstone skied a catch to Sean Dickson off Tom Helm, but Brevis saw Spirit home alongside James Coles (9), striking back-to-back fours to first reach his half-century and then end the match.
Phoenix reached what appeared to be a competitive score after being put into bat, with opener Joe Clarke scoring 73 from 42 deliveries and Dickson hitting an unbeaten 51 from 28.
The pair put on a third-wicket stand of 92 after Mitch Owen, Joe Weatherley and Laurie Evans had all fallen for single figures, while Clarke ultimately departed from the 91st ball of the innings, caught by Livingstone off Henry Crocombe.
Phoenix's sixth defeat in seven matches mean they stay bottom of The Hundred standings, while Spirit moved level with sixth-placed Southern Brave on eight points, but remain beneath them by virtue of an inferior net run-rate.
What's happening on Monday?
Nottingham is the venue for Monday's action in The Hundred with Trent Rockets hosting Southern Brave.
The match for the women's side at 15:00 BST is a top-of-the-table clash, with leaders Rockets aiming to clinch their place in the Lord's final.
Victory over Brave in their final match would secure their spot, although given they have a superior net run-rate they could go directly to Lord's even if they lose.
Second-placed Brave are in a strong position to secure a place in the Eliminator - and would be certain if they win.
The Rockets' men's side will also secure their spot in the final on 16 August with victory over Brave in their match which gets under way at 18:00.
Brave are playing for pride, having already been eliminated and victory would guarantee they avoid the wooden spoon.

title: 'Celtic fans are going to fall in love with him' - Hogh makes his mark
summary: Kasper Hogh earns rave reviews after his first goals - and first hat-trick - for Celtic in Saturday's 5-1 thrashing of Kilmarnock.
full_text:
'Celtic fans are going to fall in love with him' - Hogh makes his mark
- Published
Reminding some of the once viral Techno Viking, Kasper Hogh is already earning rave reviews after recording his first goals - and first hat-trick - for Celtic.
Big-money signings come with big expectations and the Scottish champions' record-breaking summer recruit put in a statement performance in Saturday's thumping 5-1 win over Kilmarnock.
The £11m striker had his side ahead in just 64 seconds and, with little more than half an hour played, he had already earned the match ball, a firm back-post header having been followed by a precise low finish before a diving header completed a rapid-fire treble.
Although Daizen Maeda had managed the feat in cup ties, this was the first hat-trick from a Celtic forward in the league since October 2022, when James Forrest hit three against Hibernian.
Unsurprisingly, it's already drawing comparisons between the new number nine and the heroes of the past.
The Danish forward has only played 175 minutes of competitive football for Celtic so far, but the signs are already hugely encouraging and Premiership defences have been put on notice that a proven goalscorer has arrived.
'A total and utter natural goalscorer'
Hogh had drawn some criticism for failing to show a finishing touch against Dundee in Celtic's Premiership opener, but he didn't take long to put that experience behind him when he rose to nod in Arne Engels' cross from close range while some fans were still taking their seats at Rugby Park.
The goal impressed BBC pundit Pat Nevin, who noted it as "an easy goal, but a good goal and that's where strikers want to live".
The former Scotland winger watched Hogh find space to add two more and believes there's already evidence that the defending champions have a real talent on their hands.
"Hogh is a new star," Nevin said. "And the Celtic fans have got someone they are going to fall in love with because he looks to me like a total and utter natural goalscorer, as well as a good technical player as well.
"Celtic loved Daizen Maeda with his workrate, and before that Kyogo Furuhashi, but this guy looks like he can fill those shoes with some ease.
"I can remember watched Kyogo in his first game and thinking 'Oh, my word, you could be the new Larsson' because of his movement and he's that good.
"After 45 minutes, I'm looking at Hogh and thinking this isn't a fluke. Some players can come in and get a hat-trick and it's a bit lucky because you find yourself in the right position.
"No, this is a player, this is a striker who knows where the goal is, knows where to go, has intelligent movement and there's his link-up play as well."
BBC Scotland's chief sportswriter, Tom English, was equally impressed and saw a striker who can "tear up this league".
"Hogh is looking more ruthless than he did on Monday, when he had chances and didn't take them," he said.
"In my opinion, he is the most proven goalscorer that Celtic have signed since Chris Sutton. I'm talking about pedigree, who has done it before he got to Celtic.
"Look at the goals he's scored in the Champions League against Atletico Madrid, Manchester City, Inter Milan and for Bodo/Glimt against Sporting, Olympiacos and Porto.
"I think it's £11m very well spent and this guy is going to get buckets of goals this season. He's a six-yard-box striker, not exclusively, but he gets a lot of his goals there and in this league against the defenders he's coming up against, he's going to tear up this league."
Tougher tests lie ahead
Speaking to Sky Sports after the final whistle, Hogh laughed as he put his exploits down to "shooting practice", but he already had a strong scoring record from his time in Norway, where he was Bodo/Glimt's top scorer in the last two seasons and built a wider reputation as Kjetil Knutsen's side made a splash in Europe.
It's that balance of sustained goalscoring across both domestic and European football that Celtic are hoping to get from the 25-year-old.
After the goals that drew him level with St Mirren midfielder Killian Phillips as the top scorer in the Premiership at this early stage, his next challenge is to help his side progress in the League Cup before the crucial Champions League play-off tie against LASK.
Sunday's hat-trick is a start on repaying the record outlay that Celtic made to bring him to Glasgow, but the club is eyeing progress in Europe and the riches the Champions League can lavish on the club will easily exceed what was paid for the forward.
If Hogh can help the team to success at the elite level, where he has already shone against the biggest names, comparison with great Celtic strikers of the past is guaranteed.

title: No Dogs in Space is a music history podcast for true obsessives
summary: Sadly, there hasn't been a new episode of No Dogs in Space since July of 2024. Part four of the podcast's series on Can wrapped up an abbreviated season three, which focused on experimental rock. Don't get me wrong, I loved seasons one and two, but the show seemed to be gearing up for a […]
full_text:
Sadly, there hasn’t been a new episode of No Dogs in Space since July of 2024. Part four of the podcast’s series on Can wrapped up an abbreviated season three, which focused on experimental rock. Don’t get me wrong, I loved seasons one and two, but the show seemed to be gearing up for a deep dive into Krautrock, and I was hype. Unfortunately, that episode ended with hosts Marcus Parks (Last Podcast on the Left) and Carolina Hidalgo declaring they were going to do another season on punk (the topic of season one), only for the feed to go quiet.
No Dogs in Space is a music history podcast for true obsessives
Now if only they’d give us some new episodes.
No Dogs in Space is a music history podcast for true obsessives
Now if only they’d give us some new episodes.
If you’re a music obsessive, this is a must-listen podcast. Over the course of 73 episodes, the husband-and-wife duo digs into the careers of the Beastie Boys, The Velvet Underground, Joy Division, and more. Even if you think you know everything there is to know about iconic bands like The Stooges, I guarantee there will be new info here.
The show dedicates multiple hours over the course of several episodes to its subjects. Its two-part intro to Krautrock, which heavily focuses on Amon Düül II is over three hours long, and that’s on the shorter side. The Replacements series is nearly nine hours long, and Beastie Boys is even longer still.
Over these exceptionally long series, it never gets dull, though. The two balance scripted info-dense sections with more improvisational sidebars expertly. They also, as you’d expect from a married couple, have great chemistry on mic. They also make sure to share all their sources at the end of the episode in case you want to track down the primary source or do your own fact-checking.
The show isn’t officially over. As recently as a couple of months ago, Carolina was responding to Instagram comments saying she’d love to do more episodes. And the possibility of the show returning has come up multiple times on live streams. But as of this writing, we’re still waiting on that Punk Rock 2.0 series.
No Dogs in Space is available on most podcast platforms, including Apple Podcasts, Pocketcasts, and Spotify.

title: McInnes left frustrated amid Rangers' poor start to season
summary: Derek McInnes is still seeking a win after three games as Rangers managers and feels hard done by following a 2-1 home defeat by Hibernian and injury to big-money striker Youssef Chermiti.
full_text:
McInnes left frustrated amid Rangers' poor start to season
- Published
Nine days, three games, zero victories and five goals conceded - Rangers are yet to get going under Derek McInnes.
Dundee United, Jagiellonia Bialystok and now Hibernian have all taken first-half leads against the Ibrox side as they struggle to find a semblance of form during a rocky start to the campaign.
While issues persist across the park, from their profligacy in front of goal to their inability to penetrate organised defences, their continued defense lapses will undoubtedly be a growing cause for concern.
As former Hibs midfielder Scott Allan said on BBC Radio Scotland after the 2-1 home defeat by his former side: "Based on today, I'd be very surprised if Derek McInnes knows what his best 11 is and we're into the big games already - and that's a problem."
- Chermiti injured after Rangers reject bid for striker 
  - Published45 minutes ago
'No consistency in how Rangers play'
After their Europa League qualifying loss in Poland, McInnes called on his side to "be far more stingy with our work, defend the goal with our lives, don't give our opponent opportunities" and criticised the squad for showing the same worrying characteristics that were the club's ruin last season.
His side showed little sign of turning this around in the short space of time since their European trip.
Against Hibs on Sunday afternoon, his third different back four of the season struggled to hold their shape and summer signing Vanja Dragojevic soon grappled Josh Kerr to the ground for a penalty as the errors continued.
These faults, coupled with a lack of consistency in playing partners, is compounding the misery.
Their draw with Dundee United started with a back-line comprising of Ben Godfrey, Dujon Sterling, Emmanuel Fernandez and Tuur Rommens.
Away in Poland, it was Ross McCrorie, Sterling, Emmanuel Fernandez and Rommens.
When David Gray's team came to town it was Dragojevic, Olwethu Makhanya, Fernandez and Rommens.
These issues need to be ironed out quickly by the coaching staff as their Europa League qualification hangs in the balance prior to Thursday's second leg against Jagiellonia Bialystok.
McInnes thought the defeat by Hibs was "really harsh on us" as "we were the better team" and "deserved far better than we got" in a game in which Hibs took the lead through a penalty he disputed.
"It's damaging in the sense that we came here to win and we expect to win," he said.
"What we've got to do now is just dust ourselves down because that was a blow for us.
"The response of the team in the latter part of the game was terrific."
Their selection inconsistency is mirrored in their form on the park too.
Allan added: "Performing consistently is what [brings] results and winning silverware, and I know its very early on, but there is no consistency in how Rangers were playing today."
'Serious questions for Rangers'
A McInnes side throughout his spells in charge of St Johnstone, Aberdeen, Kilmarnock and Hearts could all be described as hard to beat.
This early iteration of his Rangers squad are the opposite.
The 55-year-old has now lost more home league games in charge of Rangers as he did in his whole time as Tynecastle boss.
As former Ibrox midfielder Ryan Jack suggested: "For Rangers to be at home in their first league home game of the season, Derek McInnes' first home game in charge and to score thtough a Hibs own goal and not create too much with two strikers on the park will be frustrating.
"I touched on it before the game, if you go one without a win it's trouble, then two, now three, usually that's crisis time and people start asking serious questions.
"It's early on in Derek McInnes' reign and a lot of new players are in, so you need time for that to gel, but as you do that, you need to pick up results as this football club demands it."
With nine signings already in the building, McInnes wants to further bolster his squad.
With Youssef Chermiti being taken off on a stretcher on the day it was revealed Rangers had rejected a big-money offer for the striker, that may complicate matters further.
Especially as it appeared that another winger and extra defenders were the manager's priorities.
Speaking pre-match, the manager said: "We've got a few bids in for several players and a few things are ongoing at the minute.
"Ideally, a lot of these things would have came to fruition a wee bit quicker.
"But hopefully, if there is any news to tell, it'll be in the upcoming days on a few of our targets."

title: Germany warns of ‘daily hybrid warfare’ after explosive-laden drone found
summary: Espionage, sabotage, cyberattacks, and covert operations are a 'constant reality', says Germany's interior minister.
full_text:
Germany warns of ‘daily hybrid warfare’ after explosive-laden drone found
Espionage, sabotage, cyberattacks, and covert operations are a ‘constant reality’, says Germany’s interior minister.
Germany is facing daily “hybrid warfare” attacks from abroad, an official has said, days after an explosive-laden drone was discovered at Leipzig/Halle Airport.
Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told the local newspaper Bild am Sonntag on Sunday that foreign powers wanted to subdue Germany politically and socially by stirring up fear.

- list 4 of 4Bulgaria, Germany drone incidents raise security fears amid Ukraine war
“We’re not at war, but we are the daily target of hybrid warfare,” Dobrindt said.
“Espionage, sabotage, cyberattacks, or covert operations by foreign powers aimed at destabilising Germany or inflicting direct harm are a constant reality.”
He did not identify any countries behind the alleged attacks.
The minister’s comments come after a drone loaded with explosives was discovered at the Leipzig/Halle Airport in eastern Germany on Tuesday.
Some German lawmakers pointed the finger at Russia, which has been at war with Ukraine since its full-scale invasion of the country in 2022.
The Russian embassy in Berlin on Friday dismissed the Leipzig event as a “fabricated provocation”, saying it was another example of unsubstantiated accusations against Moscow.
Germany plans to boost anti-drone capacity
Germany is planning to strengthen its ability to counter drones amid concerns over the threat, Bild reported, citing government sources.
The newspaper said Dobrindt’s ministry wanted to double the federal government’s team of anti-drone experts from 150 to 300 and increase its network of related bases from four to eight.
Germany’s armed forces said on Saturday that two drones were spotted late on Thursday over a German military base site in Mechernich, in the western state of North Rhine-Westphalia.
Separately, a drone exploded on Saturday in Bulgaria near the Trans-Balkan gas pipeline.
Bulgaria’s defence ministry said there was no reason to suspect the incident was intentional. Ukraine said it was working with Bulgarian authorities to clarify the circumstances.
The drone incidents across Europe have renewed concerns that Russia’s war in Ukraine could increasingly affect neighbouring NATO states.
NATO and European Union officials have blamed Russia for previous drone sightings. Russia has rejected all the allegations.

title: Why Malaysia’s political turmoil matters to Beijing
summary:
As China seeks to reshape the global order, Malaysia’s political instability offers a cautionary tale about the challenges Beijing may face abroad.
A recent Pew Research Centre survey found that global perceptions of China have improved relative to those of the US, driven partly by the view among some respondents that China under President Xi Jinping is more reliable than a US led by President Donald Trump. As Washington retreats from global leadership roles, Beijing has sought to present itself...
full_text:
Advertisement
Opinion
Why Malaysia’s political turmoil matters to Beijing
Malaysia shows how local battles over race and national identity could complicate China’s Southeast Asian playbook
3-MIN READ3-MIN
Peter TC Chang is a research associate at the Malaysia-China Friendship Association and a former deputy director in the Institute of China Studies at University Malaya. 
As China seeks to reshape the global order, Malaysia’s political instability offers a cautionary tale about the challenges Beijing may face abroad.
A recent Pew Research Centre survey found that global perceptions of China have improved relative to those of the US, driven partly by the view among some respondents that China under President Xi Jinping is more reliable than a US led by President Donald Trump. As Washington retreats from global leadership roles, Beijing has sought to present itself as the architect of an alternative vision that, it argues, better reflects the aspirations of the developing and non-Western world.
At the centre of this ambition are Xi’s four global initiatives: on development, security, civilisation and governance.
Malaysia has emerged as an important partner in these efforts, particularly Xi’s Global Civilisation Initiative. Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim and Xi have promoted dialogue between Confucian and Islamic traditions, reflecting a shared interest in advancing a more pluralistic global order rooted in civilisational understanding. The idea also resonates with Anwar’s long-standing vision of an “Asian Renaissance” – a belief that Asia’s great civilisations should reclaim their intellectual and cultural influence in shaping the emerging Asian century.
Yet, Anwar’s vision faces profound domestic challenges. In recent weeks, his multi-ethnic governing coalition suffered two consecutive defeats in state elections – first Johor, then Negeri Sembilan – following campaigns dominated by racial and religious appeals.
Malaysia’s two major Malay-based parties, Umno and PAS, united around a familiar message: that Malay and Muslim interests could only be protected through greater political solidarity among Malays against non-Malay parties.

title: 'Spectacular' Game of Thrones stage spin-off opens at home of Shakespeare
summary: The verdict from most theatre critics is that it's a worthy addition to the epic fantasy franchise.
full_text:
'Spectacular' Game of Thrones stage spin-off opens at home of Shakespeare
- Published
The first Game of Thrones stage spin-off has been launched by the Royal Shakespeare Company, and the verdict from most theatre critics is that it's a worthy addition to the epic fantasy franchise.
Game of Thrones: The Mad King, a prequel set shortly before the events of George RR Martin's first book and the all-conquering TV series, officially opened at the RSC in Stratford-upon-Avon this weekend.
The Telegraph awarded four stars to the "spellbinding spectacle", while the Guardian's four-star review said it features "spectacular stagecraft and plenty of modern resonance".
The Times was more lukewarm, giving three stars and saying the play "lacks pace, sex and gore".
The Game of Thrones origin story is epic in both ambition and execution – it has taken seven years to reach the stage, clocks in at three hours 45 minutes, and features a 36-strong cast.
The characters include younger versions of familiar figures like Ned Stark, Jaime Lannister and Robert Baratheon; and others whose fates were key to the events in the main saga, such as Lyanna Stark, Prince Rhaegar Targaryen and the "mad king" himself, Aerys II Targaryen.
After opening in Shakespeare's home town, the RSC will hope it can go on to replicate the success of other spin-off plays like Harry Potter and the Cursed Child and Stranger Things: The First Shadow, which have both had lengthy runs in the West End and on Broadway.
The Shakespeare connection stems from the fact Martin's novels were heavily inspired by Shakespeare's history plays, especially those about the battles between the houses of Lancaster and York during the Wars of the Roses in the 15th Century.
Game of Thrones' US creator was heavily involved in the play, stationing a representative in rehearsals at all times, and he attended the opening night in Stratford on Saturday.
In his review, the Guardian's Mark Lawson wrote, external: "Purists will object that, rather than staging Shakespeare-adjacent populist spin-offs, the RSC should be offering its house dramatist's royal dramas plain.
"The counter argument is that hitching on to a cultural juggernaut may bring in new sources of income and audiences."
Audiences will respond differently to the play depending on whether they are already loyal Game of Thrones fans, which Lawson's four-star rating reflected.
"This feels like a five-star production for most devoted throners but a three-star for those who haven't seen the TV series," he said.
Metro's critic Dave Freak agreed, external, also bestowing four stars.
"As a stand-alone piece of theatre, The Mad King scrapes through," he wrote. "But as an extension of the Game of Thrones world, it scores well, shifting the narrative to the stage with suitably theatrical thrust."
'Lacks grit, gore and nudity'
The Telegraph's Dominic Cavendish wrote, external: "At almost four hours, it's a long evening, sometimes too dense with detail, and it lacks the grit and gore (not to mention the nudity) of the TV series.
"Still, it capably serves newbies and devotees, and speaks in a timely fashion to our age of unruly leaders."
He added: "It's not up there, yet, with the Harry Potter or Stranger Things prequels but, on balance, the Game of Thrones franchise has yet another worthwhile and lucrative spin-off on its hands."
The Times' critic Clive Davis, external had greater reservations, writing that while the play "gives hardcore GoT fans a chance to go hunting for 'Easter eggs', it seldom comes close to matching the grim aura of the TV series".
"Duncan Macmillan's script is sorely lacking in poetry. Events plod forward, one after the other, and although Michael Shaeffer is a thoroughly compelling presence as the cruel and chronically unstable monarch Aerys, other performances seem nuance-free. Too many lines are simply shouted. You expect better of the RSC."
Davis concluded: "It goes without saying that there are more than enough GoT devotees to keep the box office ticking over for the rest of eternity, but only the most dedicated of them will have the energy for this marathon."
Others were more enthusiastic, and Whatsonstage's Sarah Crompton's five-star review, external said the play is "a triumph; a soaring, surging spectacle and a latter-day history play, both serious and popular".
She added: "It is a remarkable achievement, wonderfully directed by [Dominic] Cooke and superbly acted by every member of the 35-strong ensemble. The result is a brilliant exhibition of how theatre can create magic."
The Independent's Alice Saville, external, awarding four stars, said the "stellar stage show has all the thrillingly staged battles, gory deaths and, yes, dragons that the most bloodthirsty fan could hope for".
"But there's also a surprising amount of heart – of the warm, still-beating kind – as it lingers on the faces of its fallen," she said.
The play begins more than a decade before the events in the first book and TV series, opening with the tourney at Harrenhal, a great jousting tournament where the houses of the Seven Kingdoms gathered and where key events in the Game of Thrones legend took place.
Macmillan said he wanted to create something "on the scale of a Shakespearean tragedy and a Shakespearean history".
The playwright told BBC News: "The challenge was writing something for a fan base who take this world and their characters very, very seriously and know so much about it, and also the complete newbies, and writing something that is going to work for both of those people.
"Making something that is going to knock the socks off of everybody has been a real challenge. It's taken a long time, but I think we've got there."
Cooke said there were "lots of similarities" with Shakespeare, especially themes of "dynastic struggle, what it means to have power, intergenerational conflict and powerful families".
Martin has been "very supportive" in the process of creating the play, the director added.
"He's been collaborative in terms of the development of the script. We've worked very closely with him. And George, I think, picked up quite quickly that we were very serious about honouring what he'd done."
Tamara Harvey, the RSC's co-artistic director, said: "George himself talks about how Shakespeare and the Wars of the Roses inspired him to write these stories.
"So the connections feel very deep, and of course themes are shared: power, love, succession, battles for who gets to rule who – it's all there in the Shakespeare history, just as it is in Game of Thrones."
Asked about future plans for the play, Harvey replied: "We're hoping as many people as possible get to see it, and that starts here in Stratford. And from then, who knows?"

  - Published18 February
  - Published20 May 2019

title: Crews battle wildfires in western U.S. and Canada
summary: There have been 183 new wildfires, including eight large ones, across the U.S. since Saturday, the National Interagency Fire Center reported on Sunday.
full_text:
Crews battle wildfires in western U.S. and Canada
Evacuation orders are in place across parts of the Western U.S. and Southwest Canada as extremely hot and dry conditions fuel the spread of wildfires in the region.
There were 183 new fires, including eight large ones, across the U.S. since Saturday, the National Interagency Fire Center reported on Sunday. More than 30,000 personnel with over 640 crews were assigned to the fires. Firefighters were battling more than 94 large fires across the country, the agency also said.
Evacuations are in place across Utah, where close to a dozen active wildfires have scorched more than 300,000 acres, as of Sunday evening. The Rocky Canyon Fire, some 30 miles northeast of Salt Lake City, grew to more than 2,800 acres since it began on Friday and is 0% contained, as of Sunday — leading to evacuations in Morgan County.
Two pilots died on Friday after their helicopter crashed while battling the Widemouth 2 Fire in Fishlake National Forest, the U.S. Forest Service confirmed Sunday.
Utah Gov. Spencer Cox mourned their deaths in a social media post: "They put themselves in harm's way to protect our state and gave their lives in that service."
The Widemouth 2 fire has scorched more than 118,000 acres, becoming the largest fire in the state this year, surpassing the Babylon Fire which has burned over 107,000 acres. The fire was 27% contained as of Sunday morning.
In Oregon, a bulldozer operator identified by officials as Jason Ensign, died battling the Wrights Spring Fire, which has spread over 33,000 acres and was 0% contained as of Sunday afternoon.
Large fires are also burning in Washington state, Idaho, Montana and Colorado.
At least 60,000 people were evacuated in the Spokane, Wash., area as firefighters work to contain several fires that have scorched over 10,000 acres. Local fire officials on Sunday said that "crews made exceptional progress" on containing the fires and were working to ensure there are "no remaining heat sources posing threats."
"An abnormally dry and warm winter has led to an extremely difficult fire season," said the U.S. Forest Service Fishlake National Forest.
In Canada, there were more than 100 active wildfires in the country's British Columbia province, according to the British Columbia Wildfire Service. High temperatures and wind gusts are expected to linger across the southeastern parts of the province and the Okanagan region on Sunday.
"We are expecting a high potential for lightning-caused wildfire starts, particularly in the central Interior and the Okanagan which are receiving limited precipitation and dry lightning," the service said in an update on Sunday. "New ignitions occurring during periods of hot and dry weather can establish and spread quickly."
A state of emergency has been declared in the British Columbia province where the Bald Range wildfire has prompted more than 20,000 people to evacuate.
"At every step, we're focused on ensuring that emergency crews have the tools they need to protect people," said British Columbia Premier David Eby on social media.

title: Demi Vollering wins Tour de France for the 2nd time
summary: Vollering, who first won the competition in 2023, finished the stage more than a minute ahead of Spaniard Paula Blasi Cairol and 2024 champion Polish rider Katarzyna Niewiadoma-Phinney.
full_text:
Demi Vollering wins Tour de France for the 2nd time
After winning the Women's Tour de France for the second time on Sunday, Demi Vollering tried hard to hold back tears while the Dutch national anthem played.
It was her toughest moment of the day after an ultra-dominant performance on the bike from the 2023 champion.
She secured an impressive stage win, and in doing so extended her overall lead over Polish rider Katarzyna Niewiadoma-Phinney to 1 minute, 18 seconds clear of the 2024 champion.
Vollering raised her bike in the air moments after crossing the finish line in Nice. Niewiadoma-Phinney had started Sunday's ninth and final stage only eight seconds behind Vollering, who got a time bonus for winning it.
Finally, as the Dutch anthem ended, a lone tear trickled down the side of Vollering's face. A few more soon followed as her achievement hit home.
"It's not only the dream of winning the Tour de France. It's also the dream of living this life, of working hard along with passionate people," the 29-year-old Vollering said. "It all starts with dreaming. Go chase the dreams and don't let anyone stop you."
Nobody could on Sunday.
Knowing that she was well clear, Vollering began to celebrate as the line approached, raising her arm in triumph and then tapping her head with her finger to show her mental strength.
"I was thinking about a lot of things as I was approaching the finish line. I thought that I had never won in the yellow jersey before," Vollering said. "I thought about how much work has gone into this victory. I thought about the people who have been behind me."
She finished the stage 1 minute, 4 seconds ahead of Spaniard Paula Blasi Cairol and Niewiadoma-Phinney, who looked tired but was all smiles later on the podium.
Former Giro d'Italia champion Elisa Longo Borghini of Italy was third overall in the Tour — 4:29 behind — after Marlen Reusser lost valuable time after crashing going downhill after the second of the day's four climbs.
Reusser ended up 14th overall at nearly 26 minutes behind.
Vollering attacks
Niewiadoma-Phinney had it all to do on the final climb, especially with her rival sitting on her wheel, and was unable to pressure Vollering.
Vollering attacked about 800 meters from the top and dropped Niewiadoma-Phinney — as she did when winning Saturday's eighth stage to take the overall lead from her rival.
Two years ago, Vollering missed out on Tour victory after finishing an agonizing four seconds behind Niewiadoma-Phinney on the last stage.
She made full amends this time.
Vollering has now won five Grand Tours, including two Spanish Vuelta titles and the Giro d'Italia secured in June to join countrywoman Annemiek van Vleuten as the only other female cyclist to have won all three Grand Tours.
"I still have a lot of dreams," Vollering said. "On and off the bike."
Four climbs
Each of the first three climbs on Sunday was 7.7 kilometers long with a 5.9% average gradient. But the final ascent branched off onto a slightly different route which, even though it was shorter at 6 kilometers, had a steeper average gradient of 7.6% with one portion stretching to a grueling 12%.
It made little difference.
After winning Friday's seventh stage with an impressive solo attack of her own up the iconic Mont Ventoux, Niewiadoma-Phinney seemed short of energy and Vollering's lead was never under threat.

This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other...
full_text:
Historian Wang Gungwu on US credibility and why Xi thinks ‘only the party can save China’
The 95-year-old sinologist gives his take on the superpower rivalry, the US advantage and Taiwan, and explains why the past is so important
Professor Wang Gungwu is regarded internationally as an authority on Chinese history. The 95-year-old is best known for his explorations of Chinese history in the long view, and for his writings on the Chinese diaspora. He has been a professor at the National University of Singapore since 2007 and emeritus professor at the Australian National University since 1988. He was vice-chancellor of the University of Hong Kong from 1986 to 1995.
At one level, it is really similar to the United States and Soviet Union Cold War because both have nuclear weapons.
The question of having to fight one another and the possibility of using nuclear weapons makes it unlikely that they will fight each other. Fighting through proxies would be the same as during the Cold War.
I think military strategists would think that the way to deal with the situation when there’s US and China rivalry is to have another Cold War, and for the US to use the same methods that they used to destroy the Soviet Union.
They would destroy the China threat in the sense of undermining its power. If they can do that without fighting, that would be ideal because fighting is dangerous.

full_text:
NSW deputy premier asks for moratorium on take-home assessments for students amid AI review
Prue Car, the NSW deputy premier, has asked the NSW Education Standards Authority (Nesa) to impose a ban on unsupervised take-home assessments during a broad review of AI’s impact on student learning.
Car said she has asked Nesa to “urgently” examine artificial intelligence and move to protect student learning amid growing evidence the technology is affecting student’s cognitive development. Half of students’ HSC result is based on school-based assessments, some of which is finished outside the classroom.
She said in a statement:
Artificial intelligence has enormous potential to support teaching and learning, but it should never replace the thinking, creativity, and hard work that education is designed to develop.
The purpose of schooling extends beyond producing an assessment task. It is to build knowledge, judgment, resilience, and critical thinking over time. If students rely on AI to bypass that learning process, we risk undermining both their education and the integrity of the HSC.
Subject to Nesa’s advice, any interim changes would be applied from the beginning of term 4.
Butler confident about ‘constructive discussions’ on gambling during upcoming session of parliament
Mark Butler said evidence given before a parliamentary inquiry on gambling was shocking and the government remains set on getting legislation through parliament when it returns this week.
Butler spoke to RN Breakfast, saying the legislation proposed by the government is ambitious, but he understands concerns from the Greens and Coalition, which have both warned it does not go far enough. Labor said this weekend it was open to “sensible amendments”.
Butler added this morning:
I’m confident again over the course of this sitting fortnight there will be constructive discussions between the government and the opposition about that. Obviously, they need to tell us what it is that they want us to consider, but once they do that, I’m sure we’ll give that good consideration.
We are convinced we need to get this legislation through. I mean, it involves a very serious set of major reforms put in place by this government or proposed by this government, the likes of which the federal parliament has never seen before. We’re determined to get these reforms through.
Health minister says bulk billing rate has increased to 84%
Josh Butler
The federal government is trumpeting “big benefits” from its Medicare investments, announcing bulk billing rates across the country are up nearly five percentage points since last year.
The health minister, Mark Butler, said the national bulk billing rate for the June quarter had increased to 84.1%, announcing increases in every state and territory.
Bulk billing was up 5.7% in Victoria (to 85.7%), up 6% in South Australia (82.5%), up 4.1% in NSW (87.5%) and up 13% in the Northern Territory to 90.8%.
Other states saw smaller increases, with the ACT coming in last, with bulk billing still lagging at 59.3% – by far the lowest rate nationally.
Butler said the Labor government’s Medicare investments had helped raise that rate.
“Across the country more and more GP practices are becoming fully bulk billing clinics meaning all patients need is their Medicare card, not their credit card,” he said.
Federal transport minister ‘not happy’ after near-miss between two planes at Sydney airport
Catherine King, the federal transport minister, has asked Air Services Australia to speak with her today about a “pathway forward” after two aircraft were involved in a near-miss at Sydney airport on Sunday.
The two planes, owned by Jetstar and Qatar Airways, almost collided at Sydney airport, the nation’s busiest, on Sunday morning. A Jetstar spokesperson said its plane was following instructions from air traffic control when the pilots were forced to break “firmly” when another aircraft came within “close proximity”.
Inquiries suggest a tug vehicle pulling the Qatar jet may not have followed instructions.
The incident came after delays to more than 150 flights passing through Sydney on Saturday as the airport struggled with staffing shortages.
Airservices Australia, which oversees air traffic control, was managing reduced air traffic movements and had been unable to roster enough staff for three consecutive days, the Airlines for Australia and New Zealand chief executive, Stephen Beckett, told the ABC this weekend.

We’re not happy. No one wants to see passengers disrupted in the way they have been.

title: Burnham brings forward ban on 'subscription traps' to ease cost of living
summary: The prime minister is embarking on a UK tour with a series of announcements aimed at easing living costs.
full_text:
Burnham brings forward ban on 'subscription traps' to ease cost of living
- Published
Consumers will benefit from an end to so-called subscription traps and a crackdown on "pretend prices", Andy Burnham has said.
The prime minister is bringing forward a package of changes announced under his predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer, to make it easier to cancel subscriptions.
Burnham is also planning to outlaw shops using fake "was" prices, which he said trick shoppers into thinking they are getting better value on purchases.
Shadow chancellor Mel Stride branded the measures "reheated" and said the prime minister "has already run out of ideas".
The plans were announced under Sir Keir Starmer in April, but are being brought forward by Burnham's government in a bid to give families "room to breathe" amid the high cost of living.
Burnham, who is embarking on a tour of the UK while Parliament is in recess, has promised a series of "everyday fixes" to help people with the cost of living.
He said: "I'm determined to pull every single lever we can to provide people with some room to breathe on the cost of living."
The measures being brought forward are aimed at making it easier for consumers to cancel unwanted subscriptions and stopping people being rolled onto expensive contracts without their knowledge.
They were expected to come into force next spring, but Burnham's government has promised they will now be implemented by January 2027.
When they were announced in April, the government said the plans would save consumers £400m a year in total, or up to £170 per person.
On top of the already planned changes, Burnham is also vowing to end shops' use of "pretend prices". This will stop retailers using "was" prices, made-up discounts or misleading recommended retail prices (RRPs) to highlight deals.
The government will launch a consultation this autumn to decide how the new measures should be implemented.
Consumer group Which? said it has "repeatedly exposed businesses, including trusted household brands, ripping off customers with dodgy deals that aren't what they seem".
Its head of consumer rights policy, Sue Davies, welcomed the announcement and called for the government to bring the rules in "swiftly".
But Stride said: "The cost of living didn't become a problem last week, so you have to ask why it has taken Labour so long to enact legislation passed by the previous government."
The Digital Markets, Competition and Consumer Act, passed under the Conservatives in 2024, cracked down on hidden fees, fake reviews online and made it easier for customers to cancel subscriptions.
The announcement is Burnham's latest intervention aimed at easing the cost of living, following a £2 bus fare cap in England and a VAT cut on household electricity bills.
But he is likely to come under pressure to make more significant changes in the Budget, which will be delivered by Chancellor John Healey on 28 October.
But Healey has made it clear he will oversee "strong fiscal discipline" – which will limit how much the government has to spend.

title: Evidence that South African special forces murdered top detective shared with BBC
summary: Frans Mathipa was shot while driving - we got access to the prosecution case against eight accused men.
full_text:
Evidence that South African special forces murdered top detective shared with BBC
- Published
Senior police detective Frans Mathipa had been fighting for four months to gain access to a crucial piece of information in the case he was working on. Finally, he was told, it was going to come his way.
But he feared his pursuit of it could cost him his life.
Two days later, his car was found overturned - he had been shot dead while driving.
Now seven members of South Africa's special forces, and one military police officer, have been charged with murdering Lt Col Mathipa, a highly respected officer, in August 2023. They deny the charges.
There has been no date scheduled for their trial, and there are concerns it will never go ahead, because three of the men charged with his murder have refused to comply with a court order revoking their bail. They are still working for the army's special forces, and one of them has been promoted.
The BBC World Service has been given exclusive access to the prosecution case against all the men.
The case has caused consternation in one of Africa's most robust democracies, with fears the country's military is significantly overreaching its mandate.
We asked the South African army whether it was responsible for Mathipa's killing. It did not respond.
Several hundred pages of secret police and court documents, shared with the BBC, set out the evidence suggesting special forces killed Mathipa - who worked for an elite police unit known as "The Hawks".
We have also interviewed key sources in the police investigation - South Africa's former head of counter-terrorism in The Hawks; Mathipa's commanding officer; and Mathipa's family - to build the most comprehensive public account of the events leading up to the detective's death.
It presents a compelling case that South Africa's special forces are responsible for his murder.
In particular, police documents show that the vehicle that trailed Mathipa just before he was shot was registered to a front company for the special forces. And that tracking data found in that vehicle puts it at the scene of the shooting.
One of the men in the car, Maj Sunnybooi Wambi, the documents show, was also spotted at the scene of an alleged abduction carried out by special forces soldiers - the case that Mathipa had been investigating.
After Mathipa's death, special forces issued a chilling warning to The Hawks, the police documents say. "You can appoint 10 investigating officers; we will kill all of them," said the warning, according to police.
South Africa: Anatomy of a cover-up
Africa Eye uncovers a disturbing story of power, secrecy and murder.
Watch on iPlayer - or listen on BBC Sounds to the podcast, Special forces on trial
Special forces on trial - episode two available from 24 August.
The case Mathipa had been investigating was sensitive.
It centred on an Ethiopian man called Abdella Abadigga, an alleged so-called Islamic State [IS] militant. He had been granted temporary asylum in South Africa in 2008, but was arrested abroad in 2017.
Abadigga had then been smuggled back into the country, by the South African military and Department of Home Affairs, to be used as an intelligence asset - but had "gone rogue", according to Col Tollie Vreugdenburg, former head of counter-terrorism in The Hawks.
Abadigga had gone on to extort Johannesburg's Ethiopian neighbourhood, sources in the community told us. This money was used to fund IS, says the US government.
We asked the South African army if it had facilitated Abadigga's return to South Africa. And we asked the Department of Home Affairs if it had lied about a planned deportation of him to Ethiopia, and had instead smuggled him back into South Africa on an expired passport and refugee permit. They did not respond.
Specifically, Mathipa was investigating the allegation that special forces had then gone on to abduct and kill Abadigga in December 2022 - who the United States, earlier that year, had put under sanctions, designating him an IS recruiter and fundraiser, as well as a trusted supporter of Bilal al-Sudani, a top IS figure in Somalia.
Court documents show that after Abadigga's abduction, his phone connected to a mast near a military base. Police sources say it was used to call a number in Somalia.
The Pentagon did not respond to the BBC's question on whether Abadigga's phone helped locate al-Sudani, who was killed by US special forces in Somalia in January 2023, only a few weeks after Abadigga's alleged abduction.
We also asked South Africa's President Cyril Ramaphosa whether Abadigga had been kidnapped at the behest of the US. He declined to comment.
When Mathipa was assigned the case, four months before his own death, he already knew special forces were implicated, but he was trying to secure more evidence.
He was building on information already gathered by Abadigga's brother, Ameen - who had opened a missing person's case soon after the disappearance, and had been assigned an investigating officer (IO) from local police.
He and the IO had obtained CCTV footage showing the last known movements of Abadigga and his bodyguard Kadir Abotese at the Mall of Africa, a shopping centre on the outskirts of Johannesburg.
The footage, clips of which the BBC has seen, shows a man in a blue top following Abadigga and his bodyguard as they leave the food court to head back to the car park, and paying for parking three seconds after Abadigga and Abotese do.
The mall CCTV footage contains another vital clue. The licence plates of the suspected kidnappers' vehicles are clearly visible.
The vehicles were all registered to a company called Peters Communications Trust (PCT), a front company for South African special forces - Ameen and the IO were to discover.
At the time of Abadigga's disappearance, PCT's directors included Maj Gen Herbert Mashego, the then commanding officer of 5 Special Forces Regiment.
Police documents say a meeting was arranged between the IO and high ranks of the military, including Brig Gen Yalo, the then head of special forces, at which the IO was instructed to tell Ameen there was no link between PCT and the military.
So, with the investigation seemingly at a standstill, Abadigga's brother took his case to the Johannesburg High Court.
Responding to Ameen's legal action, special forces denied all knowledge of Abadigga or his whereabouts. They did, however, admit their soldiers had been at the Mall of Africa on the date in question, but said they had been there for a training exercise.
They named the man seen wearing blue on CCTV as Maj Sunnybooi Wambi, and said he had been the exercise commander. They also admitted all the suspect vehicles seen at the mall belonged to them.
Domestic operations by South Africa's military need to be authorised by both the government and the presidency.
We asked South African former Defence Minister Thandi Modise, and President Ramaphosa, if they had authorised a training exercise in the Mall of Africa - Modise did not respond and Ramaphosa declined to comment.
When Mathipa was assigned to the case a month later, he issued a subpoena to special forces to force them to hand over full details of this alleged training exercise and all the personnel involved.
When access to these documents was finally promised, three months later, Mathipa had a premonition that he would be murdered - according to Brig Paulina Sekgobela, his commanding officer.
"When [Mathipa] left my office he said: 'Brigadier, you know, these people - they are going to kill me. I'm going to die'," she told the BBC.
On the day Mathipa was killed, he was phoned by a man calling himself Tebogo, who claimed he had information on the case for the detective - according to Mathipa's daughter Basetsana, who was home with him at the time.
Mathipa and Tebogo arranged to meet at a petrol station in Pretoria.
When Tebogo failed to show, Mathipa drove away again, along the highway.

title: Mourinho says he agreed to replace Ferguson at Man Utd
summary: David Moyes succeeded Sir Alex Ferguson at Old Trafford in 2013 but things could have been so different, Jose Mourinho reveals in a new documentary.
full_text:
Mourinho says he agreed to replace Ferguson at Man Utd
- Published
After years of speculation, Jose Mourinho has confirmed that he agreed to replace Sir Alex Ferguson at Manchester United in 2013, before changing his mind and re-joining Chelsea instead.
"When I left Real Madrid, I signed to go to Manchester United after Sir Alex," the 63-year-old coach - now back at Real for a second spell - said in a new Netflix documentary series about his career.
"He was offered the job, yes," confirmed Ferguson, who won 13 Premier League titles over 26 years at Old Trafford before retiring in 2013.
"I sat him down and explained the situation," he added: "As far as I was concerned, he was accepting. And then, within hours, it changed."
What changed was that Mourinho felt he could not turn down a return to Chelsea, where he had won consecutive Premier League titles in 2005 and 2006.
"One night, he phoned me and he was crying and he says, 'Alex, I can't take it. I've given my word to Chelsea and I'm not going to break my word'," said the former United boss.
"The reason he gave to me, I could understand, but I was disappointed."
Mourinho said he was "very flattered" to be offered the job of replacing Ferguson "because Manchester United has an incredible appeal".
"But one thing is love for football, another thing is love for a certain club," he explained.
"I think this is more powerful than love for football and fundamentally, after Real Madrid, I needed to feel that I'm loved.
"For me to lose the chance to be the coach to succeed Sir Alex Ferguson was dramatic, but I don't regret (it) because it was a decision that I made with my heart."
After returning to Stamford Bridge in 2013, Mourinho went on to win his third Premier League title as well as the League Cup.
In May 2016, he got a second chance to take over at United, succeeding Louis van Gaal.
Over a two-and-a-half year spell at Old Trafford, Mourinho won League Cup and Europa League titles before being sacked in December 2018 following a slump in results.
He returned to another of his old clubs, Real Madrid, in May this year. Mourinho's last spell there ended in acrimony as he fell out with club captain Iker Casillas and other players.
On the eve of his Real reunion, the combative manager and former Spain goalkeeper Casillas spoke candidly about the reasons behind those differences.
Mourinho also spoke about difficulties he has faced with former Chelsea owner Roman Abramovich, who hired him twice and sacked him both times.
'The relationship I had with Jose was very cold'
After taking over a struggling Real side, Mourinho helped them challenge the dominance of Pep Guardiola's Barcelona, winning La Liga, Copa del Rey and Spanish Super Cup trophies in his first two seasons at the Bernabeu. The 100 points they amassed in 2011-12 remains a La Liga record.
However, the wheels came off in Mourinho's third season in the Spanish capital and he was dismissed at the end of 2012-13 with Real finishing 15 points behind rivals Barcelona.
His treatment of Casillas divided the dressing room. The goalkeeper made 725 appearances across 25 years at Real, winning three Champions League titles and five La Liga crowns, but had spent much of the 2012-13 season on the bench.
"The relationship Jose and I had was very cold," he said.
"In those years, I really think it was taken to a limit where in the end, the rope broke."
Former Real midfielder Sami Khedira said that Mourinho's rift with Casillas affected everyone.
"Iker is a Real Madrid legend, loved by every Real Madrid supporter. He benched him, doesn't speak to him, spoke bad about him in the media, so then this locker room was a nightmare, honestly," he said.
"After that, the relationship between Jose and many, many players was broken – like Cristiano [Ronaldo] and the Spanish guys, Casillas, Sergio Ramos. And those players were super, super important for the atmosphere in the locker room."
Mourinho claimed that the keeper had a bad attitude.
"The first three times that I spoke to Casillas, the captain, the first thing he told me was, 'I want to ask for more holidays for the national team players'," he said.
"The second time he spoke to me was, 'I would like to ask you to put the training sessions one hour later because at the time you want the training sessions, there is a lot of traffic in Madrid'. The third time he comes to speak with me was, 'We don't want to go to [the] hotel. We prefer just to meet on matchday and go direct to the stadium to play'. And in a short period of time, I realised they're spoilt."
Former Spain captain Casillas also revealed that he clashed with Mourinho over the manager's attitude towards his international team-mates who played for Barcelona.
The 63-year-old's response was unapologetic.
"There are things that I don't accept and I will never accept and when somebody doesn't respect me, it's a problem. I say, this is Barcelona, Real Madrid. When you go to the national team, then you can kiss the guy, but not now. This is war."
- What is Mourinho's managerial record? 
  - Published29 May
- Friendship with Mourinho & search for new club - what next for Smalling? 
  - Published3 days ago
'I was playing against Roman that game' – on Chelsea sacking
Mourinho was sacked by Abramovich at Chelsea in 2007 and 2015.
The veteran manager said that his former boss became increasingly interfering during his first spell at the club, including pushing for the signing of Andriy Shevchenko.
The Ukraine striker joined Chelsea in May 2006 for a then club record fee of approximately £30m, but scored only nine league goals in 48 games over a three-year spell in West London.
"Abramovich - incredible passion for football, but knowing nothing about the situation," Mourinho said.
"Shevchenko was on the table because of connections with the boss, connections with agents and I never wanted to sign him, but I never told no one, so it's also my responsibility. You want to know the player that I wanted? [Samuel] Eto'o."
Following his dismissal by the Russian oligarch in September 2007, Mourinho had a chance for revenge when he returned to Stamford Bridge in February 2010 with Inter Milan in the last 16 of the Champions League. The Italian side beat Chelsea 2-1, before going on to win the title.
"Honestly, I was playing against Roman that game," Mourinho said.
"I was playing against a guy that sacked me. I go home happy and he goes home upset. Because I know how much he loved Chelsea, I know how much he loves to win.
"But I needed revenge, because football belongs to people like me. The other ones are the intruders that don't belong. Football belongs to the players, belongs to the coaches, belongs to the fans. Football will always belong to us."

title: Union reports 108 attacks on Palestinian journalists in July
summary: Palestinian Journalists Syndicate exposes rising threats, with over 270 journalists killed in Gaza since October 2023.
full_text:
Union reports 108 attacks on Palestinian journalists in July
The July report exposes rising threats, with more than 270 journalists killed in Gaza since October 2023, syndicate says.
The Palestinian Journalists Syndicate has documented 108 attacks by Israeli forces and settlers against Palestinian journalists and media workers in the occupied West Bank last month.
The syndicate’s Freedoms Committee said in a statement on Sunday that the violations ranged from detention and beating to interrogation, obstruction of coverage and the seizure or destruction of press equipment, describing a pattern that has made it increasingly difficult for journalists to document Israeli military raids and settler violence on the ground.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Israel is ‘trying to make Palestine disappear’: The Elders
- list 2 of 3Germany warns of ‘daily hybrid warfare’ after explosive-laden drone found
- list 3 of 3What now as Israel rejects Trump’s 15-point plan for Gaza?
Brief detentions and restrictions on reporting were the most common violations, with 58 cases recorded.
The committee also documented 11 settler attacks on journalists, including physical assaults, shoving and threats, mostly while crews covered settler attacks and military raids elsewhere in the occupied West Bank, along with 12 cases in which Israeli forces fired stun grenades or tear gas at journalists, causing some to suffocate.
Six journalists were beaten, and four sustained bleeding injuries while covering developments in Gaza, including from shrapnel. Two others were detained and four interrogated about their reporting.
The committee recorded four raids on journalists’ homes or media offices, including the closure of one outlet, three cases of equipment being confiscated or destroyed, two instances of deleted footage, and two expulsions of journalists from the vicinity of Al-Aqsa Mosque.
The syndicate called for journalists to be allowed to work “free from threats, attacks and pursuit”, and demanded accountability for those responsible.
The July toll adds to a surging record already considered the deadliest in history for journalists.
Rights groups have documented that Israeli attacks have killed more than 270 journalists amid a sweeping campaign of arbitrary press detentions since October 2023.
Al Jazeera has confirmed that 12 of its own journalists have been killed in Gaza since the start of Israel’s campaign in 2023, more than any other media outlet.
