title: Vitalik 釋出 2026 版以太坊路線圖：AI 輔助形式驗證成核心，強隱私與抗量子成新焦點
summary:
以太坊的未來藍圖迎來重大更新！據以太坊共同創辦人 Vitalik Buterin 於 X 平台發布的最新貼文指 […]

〈Vitalik 釋出 2026 版以太坊路線圖：AI 輔助形式驗證成核心，強隱私與抗量子成新焦點〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
以太坊的未來藍圖迎來重大更新！據以太坊共同創辦人 Vitalik Buterin 於 X 平台發布的最新貼文指出，對比 2023 年的版本，最新的以太坊路線圖「Strawmap」在優先順序上出現了顯著變化。除了將量子安全大幅提前外，更新增了包含「強隱私（Strong privacy）」與依賴 AI 加速的「形式驗證」等全新項目，揭示了以太坊走向精簡、安全且高度可擴展的未來。
（前情提要：加密通訊軟體 Signal 正開發「免電話」註冊！Vitalik 讚賞但警告：防不了 AI 大數據肉搜，偽匿名性已死）
（背景補充：Vitalik 解析密碼學聖杯 Diamond iO：讓智能合約「完全隱身」的行星級協議）
在區塊鏈技術快速更迭的浪潮中，以太坊（Ethereum）未來的發展方向始終是全市場關注的焦點。台北時間 8 月 10 日，以太坊共同創辦人 Vitalik Buterin 在 X（前 Twitter）上分享了一份詳細的技術反思，他將 2023 年廣為人知的「六大階段」路線圖（The Merge、Surge 等），與涵蓋至 2029 年以後的最新版「Strawmap」進行了深度對照，揭示了以太坊核心開發團隊在戰略優先級上的重大轉變。
I updated my 2023 roadmap diagram to overlay where the items that were there sit in the current Strawmap ( https://t.co/9deLIQWG24 ).
In general, a lot of overlap, but:
* Some things got reshuffled in order (eg. quantum safety up-prioritized)
* Some things deprioritized (eg.… pic.twitter.com/XLdIt4kAgT
— vitalik.eth (@VitalikButerin) August 10, 2026
抗量子提前，強隱私首度列入一級目標
根據 Vitalik 的貼文分析，雖然兩個版本的路線圖在大部分項目上仍保持高度重疊，但有幾個關鍵領域經歷了重新的排序與調整。最明顯的變化之一，是因應未來運算威脅，「量子安全（Quantum safety）」的優先級別被大幅提前；相對地，VDFs（可驗證延遲函數）與許多 EVM（以太坊虛擬機）的改進則被降低了優先級，甚至部分舊方案（如 State expiry）已被更具潛力的「新狀態類型（New state types）」所取代。
更值得注意的是，2026 年版的 Strawmap 中出現了多個在 2023 年完全不存在的全新項目。首當其衝的便是被列為第一級優先的「強隱私（Strong privacy）」架構，這反映了生態系對用戶資料保護的重視程度正急遽上升。此外，路線圖也新增了「後量子時代的激進擴展」、「Blob and gas futures」以及因 SNARKs 技術成熟而得以實現的「Native rollups」。
重押 STARKs 與 AI 加速形式驗證
在技術底層的變革上，Vitalik 點出了一個極為關鍵的共同主題：以太坊未來的擴展策略，不再是盲目追求最大化「所有」鏈上活動的吞吐量，而是轉向建立具有更嚴格屬性、且能針對高負載活動（如代幣轉帳與隱私協議）進行優化的專門機制。
為了實現這個願景，以太坊團隊正願意將協議的技術未來，押注在「STARKs」與「現代 AI 加速的形式驗證（Formal Verification, FV）」之上。Vitalik 解釋，遞迴 STARKs 技術將出現在共識層、資料層與執行層等多個協議層級中；而這種深度的架構整合，唯有仰賴現代 AI 工具協助進行徹底的形式驗證，才能確保系統的絕對安全，並進一步推動協議規範的「精簡化（Lean-ification）」。
EVM 的未來：開放架構與精簡主義
除了底層技術的升級，EVM 本身的設計空間也將迎來開放。Vitalik 透露，未來協議可能會向用戶暴露非 EVM 的指令集架構（ISA），例如更現代且高效的 leanISA 或 RISC-V。這意味著 EVM 未來可能轉型為運行在這些架構之上的中間碼（IR），而非作為基層的內建功能。
「以太坊將會是量子安全的、把用戶隱私放在第一位的、安全的、抗審查的、高效能且可擴展的，同時也是精簡（Lean）的，」Vitalik 在結語中感性地總結，這份藍圖不僅是技術的演進，更是眾多以太坊研究者與開發者多年來不懈努力的結晶。

title: 世代級警告！標普 500「席勒本益比」飆破 40，重現網路泡沫極端估值
summary:
美股多頭狂歡背後暗藏隱憂？據《The Motley Fool》報導，標普 500 指數近期屢創歷史新高，但一項 […]

〈世代級警告！標普 500「席勒本益比」飆破 40，重現網路泡沫極端估值〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
美股多頭狂歡背後暗藏隱憂？據《The Motley Fool》報導，標普 500 指數近期屢創歷史新高，但一項被視為「世代級」的股市警告指標 —— 席勒本益比（Shiller CAPE）已飆升破 40，創下自 1990 年代末網路泡沫以來的歷史次高紀錄。專家警告，投資人對 AI 成長的過度樂觀可能面臨估值重置的風險，呼籲市場轉向尋求高品質且財務穩健的資產。
（前情提要：FOMO 情緒引爆美股！選擇權市場閃現極端看漲訊號，分析師警告反轉風險）
（背景補充：那斯達克拍板年底開跑 23 小時交易：美股一天只休 1 小時，向全日無休交易邁進）
美國股市正處於一場狂歡之中。截至 2026 年 8 月初，標普 500 指數（S&P 500）不僅屢創歷史新高，今年迄今更已上漲約 13%。如果這波多頭行情延續，標普 500 將在今年底達成連續四年雙位數成長的傲人紀錄，這是自 1990 年代中期網路泡沫時代以來從未見過的多頭連勝。然而，在市場一片樂觀之際，歷史的警鐘卻悄悄敲響。
席勒本益比飆破 40，歷史僅見兩次
據財經媒體《The Motley Fool》特約撰稿人 Steven Porrello 的最新分析指出，目前的股市與網路泡沫時期有著驚人的相似之處。其中最令人擔憂的，是標普 500 指數的「席勒本益比（Shiller CAPE）」。該指標以過去 10 年經通膨調整後的平均盈餘來計算，能有效平滑短期波動，被視為衡量市場估值的權威標準。
歷史數據顯示，席勒本益比過去 150 年的平均值約落在 16 至 17 之間。當該比率超過 24 時，通常預示著嚴重的市場調整，甚至可能演變成大蕭條或網路泡沫般的崩盤。然而，目前的席勒本益比竟高達 41.4，這是歷史上僅有的第二次突破 40 大關（第一次發生在 1990 年代末期，峰值約 44）。這意味著投資人為了標普 500 過去 10 年平均一美元的盈餘，付出了約 40 美元的代價，溢價幅度高達 135%。
世代級警告：AI 成長預期面臨嚴峻考驗
作者強調，席勒本益比超過 40 堪稱「世代級」的罕見事件。不過，這並不代表股市明天就會崩盤，而是反映出當前投資人對未來成長寄予了極高的期望——尤其是對於人工智慧（AI）相關的龐大資本支出能否帶來足夠回報的樂觀預期。一旦未來的企業盈餘成長不如預期，高昂的股價估值將可能面臨極其痛苦的「重置」。
專家建議：放棄炒作，回歸高品質資產
面對估值過高的潛在下行風險，投資人該如何應對？報導建議，如果市場確實如 CAPE 指標所示被嚴重高估，當下最佳的投資策略是「選擇品質而非炒作」。投資人應優先考量財務體質健康的企業，尋找具備低負債、充裕現金、穩定現金流，以及強勁盈餘表現的公司。
雖然高品質股票未必能帶來最刺激的短期雙位數報酬，也沒有任何股票能完全免疫市場大跌；但歷史經驗證明，圍繞財務穩健公司建立分散的投資組合，仍是應對未來不確定性的最佳防禦方式。截至撰稿時，標普 500 指數報價約在 7,767 點，市場是否會迎來估值修正，仍有待時間驗證。

summary:

〈比特幣礦企 MARA Holdings 上半年狂倒 2.3 萬枚比特幣！套現 16 億鎂、拋售庫存近 4 成〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
比特幣礦企巨頭 MARA（原 Marathon Digital）的倒貨規模，遠比市場想像得還要龐大！據知名鏈上數據分析帳號 The Data Nerd 於 10 日發布的追蹤指出，根據 MARA 最新提交的 SEC 財報顯示，該公司在今年上半年已悄悄出清了高達 23,093 枚比特幣，套現約 16 億美元，拋售比例直逼其庫存的四成。
（前情提要：熊底到了？比特幣礦企 PowerCompute 以 307 BTC 再融資 1800 萬美元）
（背景補充：礦企 Cipher Digital 上半年狂賣 1,619 枚比特幣！慘賠 4,770 萬鎂，急轉型 AI 資料中心求生）
比特幣礦企的「信仰」是否正在動搖？台北時間 8 月 10 日晚間，知名鏈上數據分析帳號 The Data Nerd 透過 X（前 Twitter）平台發布了一則附帶視覺化圖表的驚人數據，直指北美最大的比特幣礦企之一 MARA Holdings（前稱為 Marathon Digital Holdings），其實際賣出的比特幣數量，遠比早期新聞標題所暗示的還要驚人。
Turns out MARA has been selling a lot more than the headlines let on.
The miner offloaded 23,093 $BTC ($1.6B) in the first half of 2026, at an average of $70,631.
It still holds 35,577 $BTC ($2.3B). pic.twitter.com/aLpdLGINVa
— The Data Nerd (@OnchainDataNerd) August 10, 2026
上半年狂倒 2.3 萬枚 BTC，均價破 7 萬鎂

放棄死忠 HODL？轉向 AI 與基礎建設
值得注意的是，MARA 過去長期以來一直是比特幣「HODL（長期持有）」策略的死忠擁護者，鮮少出售其開採的比特幣。然而，隨著比特幣減半後利潤遭到嚴重壓縮，該公司的策略已出現重大轉向。從 2025 年開始，MARA 便允許出售新開採的 BTC；到了 2026 年，更進一步擴大彈性，開始從現有庫存中大舉套現。

相較於先前市場僅聚焦於 MARA 在 3 月份出售 1.5 萬枚 BTC 用於還債的單一事件，The Data Nerd 的這份總結，完整揭露了礦企在面臨生存與轉型壓力時，如何將手中的比特幣庫存化為靈活的資本工具。MARA 的策略大轉彎，不僅反映了礦業生態的劇變，也為比特幣市場帶來了不容忽視的拋售壓力。

title: New weight loss pill approved for use in UK
summary: Foundayo is made by Eli Lilly, the drug firm behind the Mounjaro jab.
full_text:
New weight loss pill approved for use in UK
- Published
A daily weight-loss pill made by the drug firm behind the Mounjaro jab has been approved for use in the UK - the first country in Europe to do so.
Foundayo, made by Eli Lilly, is for treating obesity and type 2 diabetes.
But while people will be able to buy it privately with a prescription, the approval by the Medicines and Healthcare productors Regulatory Agency does not automatically mean it will be made available on the NHS.
Foundayo is a form of GLP-1 medication that blunts appetite, and comes after the MHRA approved a pill version of a similar weight-loss drug, Wegovy, in June.
Eli Lilly said while it could immediately be used by the NHS for type 2 diabetes, it would be making an application to the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence in England for it to be recommended as a weight loss treatment as well.
Dr Simon Cork, from Anglia Ruskin University, said while the weight-loss benefits of Foundayo were less than other treatments, patients could still expect to see "significant, clinically meaningful changes to their weight".
And he said a key advantage was that it was likely to be cheaper than other weight-loss treatments, which have tended to be tightly restricted by the NHS.
University of Glasgow expert Prof Naveed Sattar agreed it was "good news".
He said another benefit was its convenience, pointing out that unlike the Wegovy pill, which has to be taken on an empty stomach, this pill could be taken at any time of the day.
"The arrival of another effective oral option is a positive development and should help more people access treatment that best suits their needs and preferences," he added.
Experts believe it could help people coming off weight-loss jabs remain slim.
Trials found that patients who had used weight loss jabs and then been given the tablet, also called orforglipron, every day for a year avoided regaining much of the weight they had lost - a known risk when coming off GLP-1 injections.
People on weight loss medication are also advised to eat a healthy diet and get enough exercise.
And, like any medication, there can be side effects to using Foundayo, including nausea, diarrhoea, constipation and vomiting.

title: MSP apologises for hurt caused by rape 'demonisation' comments
summary: Scottish Green MSP Q Manivannan is facing criticism from rape survivors groups and politicians over a podcast interview.
full_text:
MSP apologises for hurt caused by rape 'demonisation' comments
- Published
A newly-elected MSP has apologised for the hurt caused by comments in which they talked of the "demonisation" of rape.
Scottish Green Party politician Q Manivannan has also faced criticism for suggesting rape is a "spectrum of things" during a podcast recorded before they were elected to the Scottish Parliament.
Earlier, the Scottish Rape Crisis Alliance (SRCA) - which represents four rape crisis centres - said there is "no hierarchy of rape" and warned the MSP not to minimise sexual violence.
In a statement, Manivannan said clips from the podcast had been "selectively edited" but said they were "sorry" for the upset, and insisted they would never seek to diminish a rape survivor's experience.
The comments, which were made during The Subjective Space podcast , externalrecorded last year, sparked fury after they re-emerged online at the weekend.
Manivannan, who identifies as non-binary and uses they/them pronouns, was being interviewed about care and carers in society, when host Sindhu Rajasekaran raised the rehabilitation of criminals, saying she could have no empathy for rapists.
The Edinburgh-based former writer and academic said there was a "myth of the monster rapist" and "a demonisation of rape in the sense of it is a spectrum".
They continued: "It is a spectrum, none of which is any less or worse, but it is a spectrum of things that constitute one homogenised word 'rape'".
Manivannan went on to argue that the idea of a rapist as a "big burly man" was understandably a source of fear.
But the MSP told Rajasekaran that "any individual is capable of rape, including yourself and me, and I think that scary thought is the hardest to contend with".
'No hierarchy of rape'
The comments have been widely criticised by survivors groups and political opponents who said they downplayed the seriousness and lasting trauma of rape.
The SCRA, which comprises support groups in Glasgow, Lanarkshire, Ayrshire and the Western Isles, said the impacts of rape can last a lifetime, and the crime should never be reduced to a theoretical debate.
In an open letter the alliance said: "We are not demonising rape. We are naming it."
The authors strongly opposed the idea of rape existing on a "spectrum", insisting "there is no hierarchy of rape" and that no survivor should feel compelled to ask whether their experience was serious enough."
The letter urged politicians "not to normalise" rape or sexual violence, and "not create hierarchies of harm".
While not naming Manivannan, the United Nations Special Rapporteur on Violence against Women and Girls, Reem Alsalem, posted on X that rape should never be spoken about in terms of it being a spectrum.
Scotland's Children's Minister Siobhan Brown told the BBC's Sunday Show Manivannan's words were misjudged.
Scottish Labour and the Scottish Liberal Democrats have also been critical, while the Scottish Conservatives called on the Scottish Greens to suspend the MSP.
Meghan Gallacher, the party's equalities spokeswoman, said: "It is deeply alarming that anyone, but especially an elected representative, would ever seek to minimise the seriousness of rape and suggest that there is a spectrum of offences."
'Malicious' editing
In a statement issued on Monday afternoon, Manivannan said they were "horrified" that the comments had been "selectively edited in order to mislead people and misrepresent me".
The MSP said that during the interview they had categorically stated that every rape in every context is equally serious and harmful but this had been "maliciously" left out of clips.
They added: "I recognise that the words in the clip shared, without the full context of the conversation, have caused considerable upset.
"For that I apologise. I will always stand with and for victims and survivors."
Manivannan said they were themselves a survivor of sexual violence and understood the enduring trauma of such an experience.
"I would never seek to diminish or dismiss any survivor's experience, or to make anyone feel that their pain was not heard or understood," they added.
"I am genuinely sorry to everyone who has been distressed, hurt or triggered by the clips, and by the discussion and coverage that has followed.
"Words matter, particularly when speaking about something as deeply personal and painful as sexual violence, and I regret this hurt caused."

title: From Dubai to a Dublin court - how alleged cartel boss Daniel Kinahan returned to Ireland
summary: Law enforcement agencies in Ireland and the US believe he is a leading figure in the Kinahan Organised Crime Group.
full_text:
From Dubai to a Dublin court - how alleged cartel boss Daniel Kinahan returned to Ireland
- Published
Armed police took up positions at the entrances to the Special Criminal Court in Dublin, as the plane carrying Daniel Kinahan approached the city.
On the steps of the building, journalists from Irish and international media tracked the flight online.
The Irish government had sent its jet to Dubai.
It is usually used to transport ministers, but it left the United Arab Emirates (UAE) with a suspected crime boss on board.
The doors of the court opened around half an hour after the aircraft landed at a military airfield nine miles (14km) away.
As reporters went through security, we heard the sound of sirens outside - indicating the arrival of the accused.
The courtroom filled up over the next 45 minutes - as detectives, prosecutors, and some members of the public took up seats along with the media.
From the moment Kinahan entered the dock, until he was led out 13 minutes later, almost everyone was looking towards him - and the proceedings were accompanied by constant typing from the press benches.
Complex international investigations, and diplomacy, had led to this moment.
Kinahan was charged with a single offence - directing the activities of a criminal organisation between October 2015 and April 2017.
He did not have to enter a plea at this stage of the court process.
But his lawyers have previously told the BBC that the allegations he is a crime boss are false and have no evidential basis.
They also said he had no criminal record or convictions.
Law enforcement agencies on both sides of the Atlantic believe he is a leading figure in the Kinahan Organised Crime Group.
The gang began as a street drug dealing operation in Dublin in the 1980s. From there, it became an international player in organised crime.
It has been linked to drug trafficking, money laundering, and murder.
The former deputy director of the UK's National Crime Agency, Roy McComb, said the group had grown globally because it had the "ambition and drive" to do so.
McComb told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that the Kinahan group had created links with other organisations from South America, Eastern Europe, Pakistan and Afghanistan, who were involved in the "wholesale distribution" of drugs.
He said the cartel became "the go-to organised crime group to move large quantities of narcotics around Europe".
McComb explained they were "seen to be a threat to the stability of the US dollar", because they were trading in the currency.
In 2022, the US offered a reward of $5m (€4.3m; £3.7m) for information about Kinahan, his father Christopher Senior and brother Christopher Junior.
The organisation had previously come to more widespread global media attention in 2016, as the result of a vicious feud with another Irish gang known as the Hutch organisation.
During that year, Kinahan was targeted by gunmen at a boxing weigh-in at a hotel in north Dublin.
Mobile phone footage of the shooting captured the chaos and brutality of the violence.
One man was murdered in that incident. During months of gangland violence, 18 people were killed.
Kinahan left Ireland shortly after the attempt on his life.
The Irish government put a major diplomatic effort into negotiating an extradition treaty with the UAE, which was signed in 2024.
Kinahan is the second person to be brought to Ireland under the terms of the agreement.
The first was Sean McGovern, who was described by a judge to be a "senior lieutenant" in the Kinahan group.
In June, McGovern was sentenced to 24 years in jail after pleading guilty to two charges of directing a criminal organisation.
Kinahan rose to his feet, with his hands clasped in front of him, when a court official read his charge to him on Sunday.
I was sitting about three metres from Kinahan.
His appearance was slightly different compared with the well-known photographs of him.
He wore plain clothes, including a black hoodie, and glasses.
He spoke several times during the hearing, when one of the three judges addressed him directly.
His tone was polite.
He indicated he would decide later whether he would come to court in person for the next hearing on 5 October, or appear via video link from prison.
Outside the court, a crowd of more than 100 people were waiting to see a police convoy carry him away at speed.
The prosecution has formally commenced.

title: From Stonehenge to the Serpentine - satellite images show impact of hot, dry summer
summary: From Stonehenge to the Serpentine the impact on parts of the UK from a long, hot, summer can be seen from space.
full_text:
From Stonehenge to the Serpentine - satellite images show impact of hot, dry summer
- Published
With more parts of England set to join Wales as being officially declared to be in drought, BBC Verify has been gathering satellite imagery showing the impact of this year's extreme summer heat.
From historic sites and parks to reservoirs and golf courses, the hot, dry weather has changed how large parts of the UK usually look.
This year's consecutive heatwaves and above-average temperatures have had a noticeable effect - even compared with last summer which was the UK's warmest on record.
Drop in Welsh reservoir level
According to the UK government, almost all reservoirs in England and Wales are officially classed as having water levels below normal or low.
Five are exceptionally low - among them Clywedog reservoir in Powys which provides water supplies for parts of the West Midlands.
These satellite images show how more of the banks of the reservoir are visible this August compared with the same month last year.
Low reservoir levels have not been the primary cause of recent hosepipe bans and drought declarations - which are ultimately triggered by a lack of rain - across large parts of England and Wales.
The Environment Agency has reported that reservoir storage is now at 69% in England, which is below the long-term average of 82% for the time of year but higher than during last year's drought.
However, in its latest report the agency says water storage levels are above those recorded during similar periods in 2022 and 2025.
While Scotland has not been as badly affected as England and Wales, July's rainfall was below average for the south and east of the country, with many areas seeing less than half the long-term average for the month.
This has led the Scottish Environment Protection Agency to warn of "significant" water scarcity in the Borders and "moderate scarcity" in areas on the eastern side of Scotland.
Brown fairways at Open golf course
Hard and dry fairways were a key talking point at golf's Open Championship which was held at Royal Birkdale on Merseyside last month.
A side-by-side comparison shows how much greener the fairways appeared in summer 2025 compared with this year.
As the BBC reported earlier this month while domestic users face hosepipe restrictions the rules for commercial users - including golf courses - vary.
When hosepipe bans are in force sports grounds can use hoses or sprinklers - but only to water grass areas "actively used for play". For golf courses this means the greens and tees can be irrigated but the fairways cannot.
Algal blooms in reservoirs and lakes
Right in the heart of the UK capital, Hyde Park's famous Serpentine lake was closed for swimming on Monday because of high levels of blue-green algae.
Blue-green algae occur naturally, but warm, sunny and settled conditions can help blooms develop. Some can be harmful to people and animals.
A similar issue is affecting Killington Reservoir in south Cumbria. Satellite images show a visible change in the water between 24 May and 8 August, where a blue-green algal bloom has been confirmed.
Looking at the rest of Hyde Park and what is one of London's prime green spaces is now mostly brown following consecutive heatwaves since May.
It's a similar sight in south Wiltshire where the usually green rolling fields surrounding the ancient stone circle at Stonehenge have become almost as pale as the path around the prehistoric site.
As BBC Verify previously reported parts of the country are suffering from "vegetation stress" where the development and growth of plants, grass and crops can be severely affected.
Vegetation turning brown, even on this scale, does not mean the plants have disappeared or died, as grass, shrubs and some trees can recover once rainfall returns, provided their root systems remain intact.
Experts have said the combination of next-to-no rainfall and prolonged hot weather is likely to cause significant issues for the farming industry and could have an impact on agriculture and food prices in the coming months.
And perhaps counter-intuitively, prolonged dry weather can raise the risk of flash flooding when it eventually does rain. That is because parched, rock-hard ground may struggle to absorb water at first, so some rainwater may simply run off the surface instead.
Scientists also warn the UK is facing a growing risk of water shortages in the decades ahead, driven by human-caused climate change and increased demand.
Graphics by Tom Shiel

title: The transgender row surrounding the WNBA
summary: After the Indiana Fever's Sophie Cunningham said it was "common sense" to ban transgender women from women's sports, a row has emerged in the WNBA - with former NBA players saying eligibility rules mean they can enter the 2027 Draft.
full_text:
The transgender row surrounding the WNBA
- Published
The WNBA is still in the midst of its 2026 season and yet it is next year's Draft for North America's top women's basketball league that is dominating the headlines.
Why? Because some former men's NBA players have declared they will enter for selection - citing the current eligibility guidelines, or lack of, for transgender women players.
"I'm officially declaring myself a WNBA prospect," said Enes Kanter Freedom, who played 11 seasons in the NBA.
It is the latest development in a story ignited by a comment made by Indiana Fever player Sophie Cunningham, who said she wanted to protect young girls "who shouldn't have to go against biological men" in sport.
Her words have instigated protests - albeit not grand in scale - on both sides of the argument, and once again catapulted the debate around transgender women in sport into the spotlight.
How did we get here?
Last month, Cunningham, one of the league's most high-profile players, gave an interview to ESPN, external in which the conversation turned to the topic of "protecting" women's sports.
The Indiana Fever guard said she had received criticism from people who believed she "hated" transgender people, something she denied.
She said she wanted to "extend love" to everyone, but added: "I also think with that love is truth, being honest. And I want to protect young girls in a locker room, or young girls in sport who shouldn't have to go against biological men."
She later doubled down on her comments, saying it was "common sense", external to bar transgender athletes from competing in women's sports.
Her words quickly moved beyond basketball and into a wider political debate in the United States.
President Donald Trump expressed his support for Cunningham, while vice-president JD Vance said she was "inspiring".
Though the 29-year-old later said she is "not a very political person", her remarks have followed her around the country. Competing rallies from critics and supporters were organised at Indiana's games, along with small-scale protests.
The scale of the debate in the media, online and in politics was striking given no openly transgender woman is due to play, or has ever played, in the WNBA.
What do the rules say?
The WNBA operates under a collective bargaining agreement (CBA), a deal negotiated between the league and its players association (WNBPA), setting rules on matters including player salary caps, revenue sharing, benefits and overall league operations.
On player eligibility, the CBA states: "Only players who are women are eligible to play in the WNBA."
The WNBA has yet to comment publicly on the row since Cunningham's comments but league commissioner Cathy Engelbert reportedly sent a memo to teams last week in which she said the matter would be discussed at an upcoming pre-arranged meeting with team presidents.
In the memo, seen by the Associated Press, external, Engelbert said the league would "always approach this topic thoughtfully, respectfully, and in alignment with the longstanding values of our league".
She added: "Our player eligibility rules, unlike the eligibility rules of some other leagues and governing bodies, are collectively bargained. Preserving the integrity of our game and ensuring fair competition will always remain among the league's highest priorities."
However, the lack of detail in the league's eligibility criteria has been brought to light by Kanter Freedom, who finished his playing career with the Boston Celtics in 2022.
"If simply declaring who you are is all that's required, then I meet every single requirement necessary to compete in the WNBA," he wrote on Instagram, external.
Kanter Freedom, who has previously spoken out about human rights violations in China and Turkey, among other issues, added: "I know my presence on the court will stir up strong opinions. I am definitely not here to mock, make fun of, or disrespect any community or personal choices.
"I'm simply asking that the current rules be applied equally to everyone - the rules that represent the very values many WNBA players and coaches have publicly advocated for."
A day after Kanter Freedom's 'announcement', Royce White - who made three appearances in the NBA as a player and is now a Republican Senate candidate - said he would also declare for the Draft, adding: "I identify as sometimes identifying as a woman for purpose of basketball."
Whether the vagueness of the rules are by design to leave it open to transgender women or a sign of an oversight that genuinely needs tightening up is not clear.
BBC Sport has contacted Cunningham's representatives, the WNBA and WNBPA for comment.
What has the reaction been?
Cunningham's comments have become a flashpoint inside a league which has a long history of player activism on issues including race, gender equality and LGBTQ+ rights.
The players' association did not mention Cunningham by name when it eventually addressed the debate.
In a statement the WNBPA denounced "hate abuse and demonisation of the transgender community" and reaffirmed its commitment to "justice, equity, diversity and inclusion".
It called on fans to report abusive behaviour at games and added that it would continue to have "hard" conversations but it "will not be used as political pawns".
There is strong feeling on both sides of the argument. Minnesota Lynx head coach and president Cheryl Reeve, who said: "I come from a space of inclusion.
"The narrative that I think is problematic is to suggest that transgender athletes are the biggest problem in women's sports."
Reeve wore a "Trans Kids Belong" T-shirt before Minnesota played Indiana earlier this month and was seen speaking to Cunningham on court before the game.
Cunningham later said the pair had exchanged their perspectives and that the conversation ended with "love and respect".
Golden State Valkyries forward Gabby Williams said she would welcome a transgender athlete "on my team or against my team, any time".
Last month, the WNBA suspended Seattle Storm co-owner Celeste Keaton from attending the team's next five home games after an exchange with two fans, who were sat courtside displaying signs thanking Cunningham for "speaking up for girls".
Keaton reportedly confronted the teenage fans and admonished them during the game. The Storm have since apologised.
As for Cunningham, the attention has increasingly become an unwelcome distraction.
Having defended her original comments, she said recently that she now wanted the conversation to return to what was happening on court.
"I want to get back to basketball, it's always been about basketball" she said, arguing that the standard of play in the WNBA was being overshadowed by issues away from the game.
But that may prove difficult, as pressure grows on the league to clarify exactly who is eligible to play.
What are the rules in other sports?
In recent years, many governing bodies in sport have amended their rules about the inclusion of transgender athletes at the elite level, moving more towards restrictions.
Athletics, cycling and aquatics, for example, have implemented outright bans on transgender women taking part in women's events.
In March, it was announced that the women's category of Olympic sports will be limited to biological females from the LA Olympic Games in 2028.
The International Olympic Committee (IOC) says eligibility will be determined by a "once-in-a-lifetime" sex test, which would prevent transgender women and those with differences in sexual development (DSD) who have gone through male puberty from competing.
In the United States, transgender women and girls are banned from competing in women's sports categories in schools, universities and the grassroots level.
That was part of an executive order - titled "Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports" - signed by President Trump last year.
It does not cover professional sport.

title: Should Liverpool fans be worried about Iraola's fitness comments?
summary: Should Liverpool fans be worried about Andoni Iraola's comments concerning the squad's fitness?
full_text:
Should Liverpool fans be worried about Iraola's fitness comments?
- Published
For the second friendly in a row, Andoni Iraola's Liverpool threw away a two-goal lead and went on to lose the game.
In Chicago on 2 August, new Liverpool manager Iraola said the 4-2 friendly defeat against Leeds was useful as he "learned a lot of things" about his side.
However, at Anfield on Sunday against Monaco, the Spaniard was a little more candid after a 3-2 loss.
Two weeks out from the start of the Premier League campaign, Iraola's verdict was that his side had "work to do" because they could not sustain the level that he wanted for the duration of a game.
Iraola said that his side played a good first 30 minutes but "they don't have much more, in terms of the levels required to play like this".
For what it's worth, the first half against Leeds and the first 30 minutes against Monaco was the best that Liverpool have looked throughout pre-season. They moved the ball with pace, were direct, pressed with intensity and both Florian Wirtz and Alexander Isak have looked sharp.
But as the game progressed and changes were made - Iraola made nine against Leeds and 11 against Monaco - Liverpool have looked like a different team and certainly not for the better. Leeds scored four goals in 25 minutes without reply while Monaco scored three unanswered goals in 44 minutes too.
Some of the squad are still working their way back to full fitness after some time off following the World Cup while others such as Conor Bradley, Hugo Ekitike and Giovanni Leoni are sidelined for lengthy periods of time.
Uruguay defender Ronald Araujo, who can play at centre-back and right-back, is close to completing a season-long loan move from Barcelona.
On Sunday, skipper Virgil van Dijk said: "Let's see what the next couple of weeks are going to bring. Any quality we can add to the team will definitely be welcome so let's see."
But with the squad at his disposal, Iraola is adamant that the general fitness must improve if they are to play the style that he wants. Pablo de la Torre, one of Iraola's assistants, has also made the move to Liverpool and was previously the fitness coach at Bournemouth.
Across the small sample size of four games, there have been enough signs of Liverpool playing in a busy manner in the early phases of games and that intensity was evident to see during an open training session in Chicago, where Iraola used phrases like "quicker, quicker" repeatedly.
One player told BBC Sport how he felt sick after the first few sessions while the punishment for losing sides in training has been to sprint to the other end of the pitch and back.
In Chicago, Milos Kerkez said that Iraola is asking the players to "play one-on-one all over the pitch, to press high and to always be on the front foot".
Iraola's Bournemouth side ranked first in the Premier League season for direct attacks and third when it came to high turnovers.
It is worth noting that it took him 10 games to secure his first win at Bournemouth in the 2023-24 season. Any such run at Liverpool would be unacceptable but you only have to look at the way Bournemouth performed throughout his tenure to see why Iraola persisted with his ways.
His comments on Sunday were certainly concerning but he has had less than a month to work with his players and only a week or so with some. The signs are there that this team will entertain but as Iraola pointed out in Chicago, it will take time.
"I would like to say, no, on the first day, we are going to be perfect, everyone will be in place, but probably it is not going to be like this," he said, when asked if it would take a while before fully seeing his style of play. "We will have to do this as quickly as possible."

Derby 'off market' as takeover deal collapses
- Published
Saudi Arabia government official Turki Alalshikh has abandoned his proposed takeover of Derby County.
The deal with Alalshikh's Lion Sport looked set to go ahead, having been sanctioned by the English Football League (EFL) and the Independent Football Regulator (IFR).
But Derby were told on Monday that Alalshikh no longer wanted to continue with the purchase of what BBC Radio Derby understands would have been a controlling stake.
"For the benefit of any doubt, the club is now off the market," a club statement said.
"It will continue to operate under the loyal, committed and unwavering support of Clowes Developments."
In a statement on social media, Alalshikh thanked those at Derby County for their involvement in the proposed deal, but suggested the time it took to be ratified meant he had to withdraw.
"We understood that the IFR process takes time and fully respect the importance of that," he posted on X.
"But unfortunately with the season already started, it would leave us with no time to prepare the team or the club for the season ahead.
"After careful consideration, we don't feel it is right to proceed at this time without the necessary preparation in place, but we will remain in conversation with the club and see what is possible in the future."
Follow Derby County on BBC Sounds
Pre-match, post-match and topical Rams content
Subscribe and listen for everything you love about Derby
A deal for Alalshikh, the co-founder of boxing promotion company Zuffa, to take a controlling stake in the Championship club had been on the table with the football regulator since May.
An IFR spokesperson said: "The IFR has a statutory duty to thoroughly test all prospective owners of a club in the top five divisions of men's football.
"The assessment was completed in 55 days out of the 90 days allowed by law.
"The IFR had taken a 'minded-to decision' to approve the bid before the start of the 2026-27 season. This had been communicated to all parties last week.
"In every case, we must consider a broad but fixed list of matters, all set out in statute.
"This includes assessing all candidates against the IFR's test on financial soundness, sufficient financial resources, source of wealth, and honesty and integrity - including a check on any criminal proceedings or convictions, civil actions and other regulatory investigations."
The proposed deal had raised concerns among human rights campaigners, including Amnesty International, which said in June that the independent regulator faced a "defining test" over the investment.
Alalshikh, the chairman of Saudi Arabia's General Entertainment Authority - and someone who is close to the Kingdom's de facto ruler Mohammed bin Salman - has been criticised by human rights groups for his role in alleged 'sportswashing'.
Saudi Arabia has been accused of using sports to improve its image in the wider world to distract from its human rights record, treatment of women, use of the death penalty and its anti-LGBT stance.
As well as being the owner of Egyptian club Pyramids between 2018 and 2019, Alalshikh recently owned Spanish side Almeria but sold the club to an investment group from Saudi Arabia last May.

title: DRC’s Ebola outbreak began months before it was officially declared, says WHO
summary: Earlier cases of the disease were wrongly attributed to malaria and typhoid, the WHO said.
full_text:
DRC’s Ebola outbreak began months before it was officially declared, says WHO
Earlier cases of the disease were wrongly attributed to malaria and typhoid, WHO said.
The fastest-growing Ebola outbreak on record started in February, months before it was officially declared in mid-May, said the World Health Organization (WHO) as responders in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) battle the surge in cases.
Mohamed Janabi, the WHO’s regional director for Africa, told a news conference on Monday that sequencing indicated the outbreak’s start, with some cases early on wrongly attributed to malaria and typhoid.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Ebola outbreak accelerates as healthcare workers strike over pay
- list 2 of 4DR Congo Ebola health workers protest unpaid wages as deaths surpass 1,800
- list 3 of 4WHO chief: Ebola outbreak in DRC spreading at ‘unprecedented rate’
- list 4 of 4Ebola cases top 4,000 in DRC as WHO urges Ervebo vaccine trial
“So we are chasing the virus, the virus is ahead of us,” Janabi said.
Confirmed cases of Ebola in the DRC have reached 4,200, including at least 1,900 deaths, according to latest government figures.
The Ebola outbreak declared on May 15 is unlike most previous ones because the rare Bundibugyo virus has no approved vaccines or treatments. Early testing was conducted for the more common type of Ebola, contributing to delays.
The outbreak is unfolding in challenging conditions, with strikes by some unpaid health workers, threats by rebel groups, anger among long-traumatised communities and misinformation asserting that Ebola isn’t real.
Health teams travel on remote, unpaved roads and have reported shortages of protective gear, while the vast population of displaced people struggles to find reliable water sources for washing hands hygienically.
This Ebola outbreak has killed more people at a faster rate than any other, including the 2014-2016 outbreak in West Africa that is considered the worst on record with over 11,000 deaths in at least 28,000 cases. That outbreak took about eight months to reach 1,000 deaths.
Ebola is rare but highly contagious and can be contracted via contact with bodily fluids, such as blood or semen, and with contaminated surfaces and materials, such as bedding and clothing. The disease it causes is severe and often fatal.
Cases doubling in some regions
Last week, WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said Ebola is spreading faster than efforts to fight it. New cases are doubling in some hotspots, Tedros said on X after meeting with officials in the capital, Kinshasa.
Access to healthcare in the region had already been challenged by years of rebel conflict in one of the DRC’s most remote and vulnerable areas.
On Friday, the WHO recommended the start of full-scale human trials for the Ervebo vaccine, the only licensed Ebola vaccine. While Ervebo has proven to be safe and effective against the more common Zaire strain of the Ebola virus, WHO experts said early data showed it may also give some protection against the rare Bundibugyo strain.
A specific Bundibugyo vaccine is the preferred option for fighting the current outbreak, according to experts from the United Nations’ health agency. Two potential Bundibugyo vaccines are in the early stages of clinical trials on people, while a third is being worked on to get it to that stage.
Several previous Ebola outbreaks have also been declared weeks or months late, including the 2014-2016 West Africa outbreak. That was declared in March 2014, although the first human case was later found to have occurred in December 2013.

title: ‘We have no one’: Palestinians react to Israel’s rejection of Gaza plan
summary: Netanyahu's declaration has reinforced doubts of lasting calm without Israeli withdrawal, reconstruction and guarantees.
full_text:
‘We have no one’: Palestinians react to Israel’s rejection of Gaza plan
For Gaza’s residents, Netanyahu’s declaration has reinforced doubts that any deal could bring lasting calm without Israeli withdrawal, reconstruction and guarantees the fighting will not resume.
Gaza City, the Gaza Strip – Palestinians in Gaza have reacted with a mix of scepticism and frustration to Israel’s rejection of a proposed 15-point plan aimed at ending the war and setting out a framework for the future.
The United States-backed initiative includes provisions for a phased Israeli withdrawal, the gradual disarmament of Hamas, a Palestinian-led civilian administration and steps towards humanitarian aid and reconstruction.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Netanyahu rejects Trump’s Board of Peace plan for Gaza
- list 2 of 3Israel’s ‘Green Rafah’ plan aims to fragment Gaza, experts say
- list 3 of 3Israel rejects Trump’s 15-point plan for Gaza, stoking tensions with US
But on Sunday, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Israel “rejected” the plan, saying its forces will not withdraw until Hamas is “genuinely disarmed”.
For Nesma Harazin, a displaced writer from Gaza City’s Shujayea neighbourhood, Netanyahu’s statement came as little surprise, as Israel continued to carry out near-daily attacks regardless of a so-called “ceasefire” agreed with Hamas last October.
“We are dealing with an Israeli occupation army that is capable of stopping these operations, but does not accept stopping them and continues to kill the Palestinian people,” said the 27-year-old.
Rather than a “real opportunity” to end Israel’s genocidal war against Palestinians, Harazin said the proposal has been US President Donald Trump and Netanyahu’s plan “from a long time ago”.
Harazin’s scepticism was shared by Mehdi Ahmed, a Gaza City resident whose family home was among the few in his area to remain standing.
“We are under occupation,” said the 53-year-old. “As far as we are concerned, any ceasefire is temporary.”
Since the October “ceasefire”, Israeli attacks have killed at least 1,258 people, bringing the overall number since the start of Israel’s genocidal war against Palestinians in Gaza in October 2023 to at least 73,386.
Ahmed warned that even if an agreement produced a period of calm, it might not last.
“Maybe we could sit here for a year without war, but I don’t think it will continue like that,” he said, arguing that the killings and the destruction in Gaza would shape future generations.
“The generations that are coming will not accept these kinds of solutions,” he said. “People who have lost their children, their parents and their families … you cannot expect them to simply forget.”
In a statement late on Sunday, Hamas said it remained committed to fully implementing the plan. It also urged mediating and guarantor countries to “assume their responsibilities” and prevent any “violations or breaches” that could obstruct the process.
The Gaza Government Media Office also blamed Netanyahu for what it described as a reversal of the negotiations and called for international pressure to prevent further escalation.
In a statement issued on Monday, the office said Netanyahu’s rejection of the 15-point document, along with demands including opposition to an Israeli withdrawal from Gaza, represented “a clear and unequivocal reversal of the negotiation track”.
‘We have no one’
But Ahmed said his experience of living his “whole life under occupation” and “in hardship” had left him unconvinced that years of negotiations could produce a lasting solution.
“They have been talking about these points for three years … are we going to spend another seven years talking about the points?” he asked, saying that Palestinians had been left without sufficient regional and international support.
“We have no one standing behind us to protect us. Why?”
For Harazin, a meaningful ceasefire would have to include the withdrawal of the Israeli army and an end to attacks, as well as a clear path towards reconstruction and the return of displaced Palestinians.
But following Netanyahu’s declaration, she said she feared further displacement and greater Israeli control over Gaza.
“If the ceasefire plan is rejected, the Israeli occupation army will carry out harsher operations than what we have heard about before in Gaza,” she said.
“Perhaps they will ask us to displace again to the southern areas. There are no buildings left standing in Gaza City.”
For Ahmed, the possibility of lasting peace is closely tied to the balance of power.
“When you are weak, there are no opportunities, and there is no hope,” he said. “Hope comes when you are strong.”
‘Hope in God’
Unlike Harazin and Ahmed, Ramez Haniyeh sees the proposed plan as a genuine missed opportunity to “end the war and the genocide”.
Haniyeh, who was displaced to Nuseirat in central Gaza after his home was destroyed, said he believed the proposal could have helped end the fighting and “stop the suffering” of Palestinians in the territory.
For Haniyeh, that would mean more than simply an end to Israeli attacks.
“Withdrawal, then reconstruction, and living with dignity,” he said when asked what he expected from a ceasefire.
But he fears the rejection could instead bring another escalation.
“I expect them to create a new target bank, so that things will escalate and there will be more bloodshed in the coming period,” he said.
Haniyeh described the humanitarian and economic conditions in Gaza as deteriorating, with widespread unemployment and many people unable to afford basic necessities.
“The situation is very bad, and it is getting worse every day,” he said. “There are some food and drink items available now, but there is no one who can afford to buy them.”
Despite his pessimism, Haniyeh said his hope rests on faith.
“I have hope in God, but there is no hope that this war will end,” he said. “It will continue until God relieves us.”
Despite her doubts about the proposal, Harazin said she also had “hope in God”.
“As long as we are Muslims, World War I ended and World War II ended too, so we have hope that the war in Gaza will end.”

title: Sudan’s army chief holds unannounced talks on national dialogue
summary: Al-Burhan engaged in discreet consultations aiming to pave the way for a comprehensive Sudanese dialogue conference.
full_text:
Sudan’s army chief holds unannounced talks on national dialogue
Al-Burhan engaged in discreet consultations aiming to pave the way for a comprehensive Sudanese dialogue conference.
Khartoum, Sudan – Sudan’s army chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan has held unannounced consultations with political and civil society groups and figures, resulting in agreement on steps to create the conditions for a Sudanese dialogue conference, political sources aware of the discussions have told Al Jazeera.
The consultations include proposals to drop charges punishable by death against opposition leaders and to form a preparatory committee for the proposed conference.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Photos: Sudan war leaves ancient Meroe pyramids at risk of collapse
- list 2 of 3Sudan’s war threatens an ‘entire generation’s’ future, UN warns
- list 3 of 3Sudan sentences RSF chief Hemedti to death: Who’s he, what’s he accused of?
The political sources, who requested anonymity, said the consultations focused on the need for a comprehensive Sudanese conference involving key political players.
The Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) have been at war with the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) since April 2023.
Those involved in the consultations have largely agreed on the need for practical steps to create a climate conducive to dialogue, including an end to media campaigns against political opponents.
According to the same sources, a majority of those taking part have agreed on practical steps to create a climate conducive to dialogue, including halting negative media campaigns and suspending criminal charges carrying the death penalty against dozens of opponents of the army-led Transitional Sovereignty Council – primarily members of the Somoud Alliance, a political grouping led by former Prime Minister Abdalla Hamdok.
The charges against Hamdok and other political figures tied to Somoud include war crimes, inciting war against the state, and undermining the constitution. Somoud has been accused of supporting the RSF, but has always denied such claims.
No preconditions
Participants in the consultations have agreed on the need to select a preparatory committee for the dialogue conference, made up of independent, widely accepted figures with specialised expertise. The committee would determine who takes part, the agenda, and the venue and date of the conference, as well as invite international and regional parties to monitor it, according to the political sources.
Hatem al-Sir, adviser to the head of the Democratic Unionist Party-Original, said Khartoum is witnessing intensive political activity and ongoing consultations in preparation for an intra-Sudanese dialogue, with the support of regional forces.
In a post on X, he said al-Burhan had held meetings with leaders of political blocs, chiefs of native administration, Sufi order leaders, independent national figures, academics, professionals and resistance committees. The meetings focused on strengthening national consensus and reaching an agreed national project.
The Quintet – made up of the United Nations, the African Union, the European Union, the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD) and the Arab League – has also been attempting to secure an agreement among Sudan’s competing political blocs on the structure of a proposed national dialogue, but has so far struggled.
Its latest round of discussions, which began in Ethiopia’s Addis Ababa on July 29, failed to bridge differences among Sudanese parties over arrangements for the conference. Several political groups, including Somoud, did not attend the meetings.
A cosmetic process
Babiker Faisal, a leader in the Somoud alliance, accused the Quintet of retreating from understandings that had previously been reached over arrangements for the political process. Faisal described the Quintet as “no longer a neutral umbrella” for sponsoring dialogue, saying that it had strayed from the principle of Sudanese ownership of the political process.
In a social media post, Faisal said the Quintet had recently called for consultations involving alliances and individuals, some of whom, he said, “have no presence in the political arena”. He added that most participants represented parties supportive of the army, which he said contradicted pledges by the Quad – the United States, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, and Egypt – to launch a political process not dominated by either side of the conflict.
He also accused Sudan’s army leadership of seeking to exploit military developments to launch a “cosmetic political process” aimed, in his words, at bolstering the legitimacy of its authority, restoring regional and international recognition, and forming governing institutions loyal to it that would grant the army chief broad powers for an extended period.
In a statement issued Friday, the Quintet said it would continue efforts to advance Sudan’s political process through renewed consultations with civilian forces and stakeholders, seeking to narrow differences over the path ahead and reach common ground that could pave the way for a Sudanese-led political settlement.
The group said broadening the scope of consultations and ensuring their inclusiveness were essential to building trust, establishing legitimacy and reaching a shared understanding that could support a credible, Sudanese-led political process.
The Quintet also reaffirmed its respect for Sudan’s sovereignty, unity and territorial integrity and rejected parallel governing structures, while calling for de-escalation and efforts towards a negotiated, sustainable peace.
No exclusion
Separately, leading figures in the National Congress Party (NCP) – which led Sudan during the rule of President Omar al-Bashir until his overthrow in 2018 – criticised al-Burhan’s announcement that their party would not be part of the political process.
Al-Bashir had made the announcement last week, saying that an intra-Sudanese dialogue conference would be held, but that it would not include figures associated with the RSF – namely the political group Tasis – and the NCP.
Former Federal Governance Minister and National Congress Party leader Hamid Mumtaz said that equating the NCP with RSF-aligned forces was “a catastrophic mistake and a statement out of touch with a complex political reality”.
Mumtaz said it was untenable to place the RSF, which he described as “a rebel militia that hijacked the state and waged war against citizens”, on the same footing as the NCP, which he said had “sent its grassroots supporters and cadres to fight alongside the armed forces to reclaim the state”.
The politician warned against the exclusion of the NCP, citing the example of the banning of the Ba’ath Party in Iraq and what he described as its catastrophic consequences. He added that any partial political dialogue, or one dominated by any particular party, would remain isolated and be doomed to fail, and would not lead to a stable Sudan.

title: ‘They need each other’: What’s behind the new Syria-Russia accord?
summary: The Syrian-Russian agreement reflects a pragmatic approach redefining past alliances amid shifting geopolitics.
full_text:
‘They need each other’: What’s behind the new Syria-Russia accord?
The Syrian-Russian agreement reflects a pragmatic approach redefining past alliances amid shifting geopolitical realities.
Syria and Russia have spent the past 18 months negotiating the fate of Moscow’s military presence in Syria following the fall of the Bashar al-Assad regime in December 2024.
On Sunday, at least part of that question seemed to be settled after the post-Assad government in Damascus announced a memorandum of understanding regarding Moscow’s Hmeimim airbase and Tartus naval base.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Lebanon ‘detains’ former al-Assad-era general, weighs handing him to Syria
- list 2 of 3What will it take for Syrians to return to Aleppo after years of war?
- list 3 of 3As Syria marks 15 years since anti-Assad uprising, security issues remain
Russia was a major Assad ally during Syria’s near 14-year civil war which began with Arab Spring protests in 2011 and ended when the current President, Ahmed al-Sharaa, led a lightning strike on Damascus and toppled the regime. Assad fled to Russia where he and his family were granted asylum.
Under the new accord, Syria will take control of civilian facilities at the Hmeimim airbase and the commercial section of Tartus port.
The military facilities will be transformed into joint Russian-Syrian training and qualification centres, with the transition expected to be completed within three months. Moscow has yet to comment on the deal.
It marks a significant shift from the role both bases once played in service of al-Assad during the civil war which killed hundreds of thousands of Syrians and displaced millions.
However, analysts say it could represent something more pragmatic, with Damascus reclaiming greater sovereignty over strategically important facilities while Moscow preserves a foothold and avoids being pushed entirely out of a country in which it has invested heavily for decades.
“The agreement between Russia and the Syrian government indicates that both countries need each other,” Alexey Muraviev, senior research fellow in defence and strategic studies at Edith Cowan University in Western Australia, told Al Jazeera, adding that Damascus is likely “not interested in terminating its prolonged relationship with Russia”.
Russia’s military foothold in Syria
Moscow was a key Assad ally during Syria’s civil war, helping to keep the former leader in power by providing vital military support.
The Russian military intervention in 2015 helped to turn the tide of the war in favour of the al-Assad-led government. Hmeimim became the centre of Russian air operations, while Tartus provided Moscow with its principal naval foothold in the Mediterranean.
However, Russia did not interfere during the major advance towards Damascus that led to al-Assad’s overthrow in December 2024.
Following Assad’s ousting, Russian troops still in Syria gradually left the country except for those stationed at the two bases.
The Syrian foreign ministry said in a statement that the new arrangements for the bases represent a “reorganising of the Russian presence” along Syria’s coast.
“This move marks the most significant development since negotiations began approximately a year and a half ago, paving the way for a new phase in Syrian-Russian relations,” the statement read.
‘No permanent enemies, only permanent interests’
According to political analyst Ruslan Trad, a non-resident fellow at the Atlantic Council, Damascus has already moved on from Russia’s role in the war.
“Syrian President Ahmed Al-Sharaa’s government fought al-Assad’s Russian-backed forces for years, yet within weeks of taking power, it began quiet negotiations to keep Moscow present rather than expel it,” Trad told Al Jazeera.
“This confirms the classic realist maxim that in politics there are no permanent enemies, only permanent interests.”
In the same vein in which al-Sharaa has gone in efforts to strike cordial relations with Western powers such as the US – which bestowed him with the status of Specially Designated Global Terrorist in May 2013 during the civil war – Trad said the post-al-Assad government has likely calculated that punishing Russia for its wartime role would cost more than it was worth.
“Moscow controls Bashar al-Assad’s asylum, holds Syrian debt and reconstruction contracts, supplies subsidised oil and grain and remains a veto-wielding Security Council power that shielded Sharaa’s own past terrorism designation,” he added.
Aron Lund, a fellow at Century International, said there is “lots of military and civilian technology” in Syria that comes from Russia and the former Soviet Union.
“There is an old legacy of military, administrative and technical cooperation between Damascus and Moscow. It would be very painful for Syria to break that relationship completely,” he told Al Jazeera.
“It’s transactional pragmatism on both sides,” he told Al Jazeera. “Al-Sharaa’s government, chronically cash-strapped and needing wheat, energy and technical support, has visited Putin twice in Moscow since taking power.”
“The leaders of both Syria and Russia have proven themselves to be very flexible and pragmatic.” Lund said.
That is reflected in the fact that the two sides began meeting and negotiating even before the toppling of the al-Assad regime was complete, he added.
“They began to meet only some weeks after Assad’s ouster. In practice, they were meeting and negotiating just weeks after Russian jets bombed al-Sharaa’s fighters. In fact, the first agreements were made even before Assad fell, during the offensive that toppled his regime,” he said.
Sovereign gatekeeper, not ‘Moscow client’
To this end, Al-Sharaa’s government, “chronically cash-strapped and needing wheat, energy and technical support”, says Trad, has visited Putin twice in Moscow since taking power.
The Syrian president has taken pains to publicly acknowledge Russia’s role “in stabilising the situation, not only in Syria but also in the region”.
Putin has welcomed al-Sharaa and signalled support for Syria’s territorial integrity.
Moscow, Trad said, needed to preserve its “only Mediterranean military platform for projecting power into Africa and the eastern Mediterranean”, while offering “debt relief, economic cooperation and UN cover on terrorism designations in exchange”.
“So yes, both sides still need each other, just on renegotiated terms that reflect Syria’s new leverage as sovereign gatekeeper rather than as Moscow’s client,” he added.
Resisting or balancing Western meddling?
Since the fall of al-Assad, Western and regional actors have sought to use Syria’s political transition to curb Russian influence, said Muraviev.
“Clearly, there was an attempt by the US and, to some extent, perhaps, the Israelis to push the new Syrian regime to terminate Russia’s presence in Syria,” he said.
“But … an agreement means that the Syrian government has retained an interest, and withstood the pressure from other parties, because they clearly see the dividends of maintaining the relationship with Russia.”
The prolonged negotiations between Damascus and Moscow were themselves telling, he said.
“The fact that those negotiations were held for about a year and a half meant that both sides were interested in not seeing these negotiations collapse,” he added.
Nevertheless, Muraviev stressed that keeping Russia in the picture does not mean Syria will close off avenues to other powers: “The new government would be open to develop strategic links with the US, Turkey, even working with Israel,” he said.
“But they would probably want to keep a multi-vectoral engagement … and having Russia in the equation will help them to use it as perhaps even a bargaining chip in their power game with other major powers.”
Lund noted that negotiations have been “very discreet”, perhaps because Russia and Syria appear to have been concerned that “talking too much about the bases” could trigger US and European demands for their closure.

title: Oil prices, stocks surge as Hormuz closure drags on
summary: US petrol prices dropped nine cents last week but could again surge if the strait closure continues, analysts warn.
full_text:
Oil prices, stocks surge as Hormuz closure drags on
US petrol prices dropped nine cents last week but could again surge if the strait closure continues, analysts warn.
Oil prices are surging as hopes dwindle that the Strait of Hormuz may reopen. The increase follows a dip last week as Tehran called on the United States to meet several demands, including ending military threats and sanctions, as well as providing compensation in order to reopen the strategically important waterway.
On Monday, Brent crude futures rose more than $2 amid Iran’s push. Brent crude futures are up 3.3 percent for the day at $84.64 per barrel. US West Texas Intermediate crude futures are also on the upswing, rising 3.1 percent to $80.63.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4AI used to create viruses not found in nature for first time
- list 2 of 4US labour market sheds jobs in July as labour force participation slumps
- list 3 of 4US Senate passes sweeping Russian energy sanctions bill amid Ukraine war
- list 4 of 4US president says he is using economic pressure, not strikes, on Iran
“Although the strait is still essentially closed, oil is currently trading at $80 to $85 per barrel, reflecting hope for a solution in near time,” SEB Research analysts said in a note to investors.
The increase follows a slight reprieve last week, with both major benchmarks falling seven percent amid hopes that the two sides were nearing a deal that would reopen the strait.
As a result, US consumers saw some relief at the pump. US petrol prices fell nine cents over the last week, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA), which tracks daily petrol prices. On average, a gallon (3.78 litres) of petrol costs $4.00, down from $4.09 last week.
But that could change soon, according to Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy.
“With the strait remaining closed, upward pressure on fuel prices could return quickly, and if things don’t go well, the national average could climb to its highest level ever recorded this late in the calendar year,” De Haan said.
“For now, enjoy the dip, but keep a close eye on how the strait situation develops in the days ahead.”
Oil and gas stocks are also increasing in US markets as the trading week begins. ExxonMobil stock rose 2.9 percent in midday trading. Chevron was up 3.1 percent, while BP climbed 2.1 percent and Shell 1.2 percent higher. ConocoPhillips rose 2.7 percent since the market opened.

title: Earthquake with 7.4 magnitude hits Colombia, killing at least 47
summary: Emergency teams are still assessing the impact of the quake that was felt across the region.
full_text:
Earthquake with 7.4 magnitude hits Colombia, killing at least 47
Emergency teams are still assessing the impact of the quake that was felt across the region.
At least 47 people were killed and dozens of buildings collapsed in cities across western Colombia on Monday after a powerful 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck the South American nation.
The quake trapped residents under debris, leaving more injured and forcing people to evacuate their homes as far as the capital of Bogota.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Death toll from Venezuela earthquakes passes 6,000
- list 2 of 3Death toll from Japan earthquake climbs to 34
- list 3 of 3UN tells world to brace for extreme weather as El Nino looms
The earthquake occurred on Monday near the municipality of San Jose del Palmar in Colombia’s Choco region, about 400km (250 miles) west of the capital, Bogota, according to the United States Geological Survey (USGS) and Colombia’s geological service. Colombia had initially put its magnitude at 6.6 on the Richter scale.
The USGS said the quake occurred at a depth of about 107km (66 miles). The US tsunami warning system said there was no tsunami warning.
“We have just experienced a major earthquake in the department of Choco. We are concerned about aftershocks,” Choco Governor Nubia Carolina Cordoba-Curi said on X. “Although the epicentre was near San Jose del Palmar, there are injuries and significant damage to buildings in the capital, Quibdo. We are already carrying out a damage assessment and will issue the first official report shortly.”
Authorities in Colombia and Ecuador urged residents in affected areas to remain alert as emergency teams assessed the quake’s impact.
In the capital, Bogota, the earthquake triggered car and building alarms as people fled into the street.
Bogota Mayor Carlos Fernando Galan said on social media shortly after the earthquake that there were no reports of injuries, and only some cracks in buildings.
“No serious structural damage has been reported in Bogota, so our resources are at the service of the country,” Galan wrote. “We stand in solidarity with the affected cities. We will continue to address this emergency and provide assistance as needed.”
News outlets aired footage of buildings also destroyed in cities such as Pereira and Manizales in a tourist region called Eje Cafetero.
In Medellin, the earthquake prompted evacuation sirens from apartment buildings, with people fleeing their homes wearing pyjamas or, simply, a wrapped-around towel. No full collapses were reported in the city, nor casualties. Medellin’s Mayor Federico Gutierrez suspended the normal operation of the city’s metro, citing necessary checks for infrastructural damage.
Small towns on the outskirts of Medellin report structural damage including caved-in roofs and fractured walls.
In Cali, which is southwest of Bogota, at least 25 buildings collapsed.
Local officials confirmed that at least 18 people had been killed in the city of Pereira, two in the city of Manizales, and 27 people in the Valle de Cauca, where Cali is located.
The quake comes weeks after two powerful earthquakes struck Venezuela in late June, killing more than 6,000 people and destroying hundreds of buildings. The tremors, measuring 7.2 and 7.5 in magnitude, were among the deadliest earthquakes to hit the region in recent years.

title: Despite Mideast wars, 20 million gather in Iraq for Shia pilgrimage
summary: Despite wars ranging across the Middle East, more than 20 million Shia pilgrims gather in Iraq shrine city for Arbaeen festival
full_text:
Despite Mideast wars, 20 million gather in Iraq for Shia pilgrimage
KARBALA, IRAQ – In the holy city of Karbala during the commemoration of Arbaeen, the story of the killing of Imam Hussein 1,400 years ago, resonates down through the centuries. It's in the plastic containers of cold water handed to sweltering pilgrims, not just for hydration but in remembrance of the water denied to the Imam and his followers before they were killed by a powerful army.
For many of the 20 million pilgrims attending this year, the killing this year of Iran's supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, and his family by Israel and the United States is a thundering echo of grave injustice against the Shia Muslims. Iran said more than three million of its pilgrims attended Arbaeen ceremonies in Karbala.
Some, like Maryam Ghanbari, showed their devotion by walking 200 miles from the Iranian border.
"More people came to Arbaeen this year because they want to avenge Agha's blood," said Ghanbari, using the Persian honorific for the slain Iranian leader. This was the ninth pilgrimage for the municipal worker from Mazandaran province.
Arbaeen commemorates the beheading of Imam Hussein in 680 in the Battle of Karbala, when the grandson of the Prophet Mohammed was killed in a dispute over who should become the heir to the faith's founder. It was the moment that caused the schism between the Shia, who followed Hussein – and the Sunnis, who gathered around his rival.
The festival is commemorated by the world's roughly 200 million mainstream Shia. Iran is the world's most populous predominantly Shia nation.
Suppressed for years under Iraqi leader Saddam Hussein's rule, the 2003 U.S. invasion of Iraq opened the door for Iraq's Shia majority to take power, including reviving ceremonies central to the Shia faith. Iran, which fought a devastating eight-year-long war with Iraq in the 1980s, turned from an enemy to an ally of the new Iraqi government.
Two decades after the U.S. toppled Saddam and oversaw his execution, Iran has a seemingly unshakeable hold on the Iraqi government and security forces. During the ongoing U.S. war in Iran, Iran-backed militias that are now officially part of Iraqi security forces have launched rockets and drones at the U.S. embassy in Baghdad and military positions in the Kurdistan region of Iraq.
Echoes of other wars
Many Iraqis, as well as Iranians, see the U.S. and Israeli war as a war against the Shia Islam.
Ali Aadi Khairi and his cousin Sajjad Haitham Latif, both 18, walked five days from the Iraqi city of Kut to get to Karbala. Two days ago, a stick attached to the large image of Imam Hussein they were carrying broke. They walked the final two days carefully holding the image between them. On the corner of the image portraying the imam with long hair and piercing green eyes were photos of Qassem Soleimani, the former commander of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, and Abdul Mehdi al-Muhandas, the late head of Iraq's Iran-backed forces. The U.S. killed them in an airstrike near Baghdad airport six years ago.
"In Iran the U.S. attacked the schools and the granddaughter of Khamenei," said Khairi, referring to the U.S. Tomahawk missile which hit an Iranian elementary school in southern Iran in February, killing 120 children, according to Iranian health authorities. Khamenei's 14-month-old grandchild was among the family members killed in the U.S.-Israel strike on his home.
For weeks before Arbeen, pilgrims set off on foot for Karbala, some carrying flags with images of Imam Hussein in the searing heat. Hospitality tents along the highways and inside cities along the pilgrimage route offer free meals and shelter. Many Iranians arrive on package tours which include bus fare and a week's stay in budget hotels in Karbala.
Inside the Imam Hussein shrine, pilgrims in men's and women's sections press against the gold and silver-encrusted latticework around the spot where he was killed, many striking their foreheads in grief. Millions of mirrored tiles reflect the crystal chandeliers and gilded walls. For Arbaeen, the lights inside the shrine and the flags fluttering from its golden dome are switched to red – the color of vengeance.
Outpouring of grief
The sound of sobbing underlays chanting in dozens of dialects woven together in a single expression of sorrow for Imam Hussein and his companions and family, killed and taken captive in the defining event of Shia Islam. Many of them call out to Hussein and his slain relatives – seen as part of every Shia's family. In the men's section, some of the Iranian pilgrims add a Persian suffix of endearment as they cry out to Husseinjan.
Outside, processions of young men in 120-degree heat carry images of Khamenei. Some hoist Iraqi and Iranian flags joined together. Some of the religious chants refer to the trip back to Karbala from Damascus by companions and relatives of Imam Hussein to reunite his severed head with his body on the 40th day of mourning in 680 C.E. The battle of Karbala is known to every school Shia child in Iraq and Iran – re-enacted every year by participants in period costumes – often with horses and camels.
On a covered walkway between the Imam Hussein and Imam Abbas shrines this week, metal fans blow a cooling mist. Shrine guards flick sticks with ostrich feathers at female pilgrims lingering too long in the shade to try to keep the flow of people moving. Medics treat heat stroke and other ailments from trailers while an announcer calls out an endless stream of names of people separated from their families.
While Iraqi Shia in particular still express gratitude to the U.S. for toppling Saddam and helping to fight ISIS militants a decade later, many now believe that the U.S. and its Gulf Arab allies are intent on destroying the region.
A show of Shia power
Naser Zadih, 38, a teacher from Tabriz, says Khamenei's killing has hardened support for resistance against the U.S. and Israel.
"It helped this movement get more depth. It got deeper and more targeted. It has helped us flaunt the power of Shia more to the face of the world to show that the Shia are building their own civilization," he says.
Asked about the economic hardship of the war, the schoolteacher says that Iranians have learned to deal with it as part of "the culture of resistance."
Like the Iranian government, he says the U.S. is not interested in negotiations. "We can talk to someone who actually wants to talk," he says.
Iranians on religious pilgrimage are disproportionately supporters of the country's Islamic regime. In upscale hotels in Karbala, a city some 55 miles south of Baghdad, wealthier Iranians dressed in black fill the lobbies. None of those asked will speak to U.S. media. One man says he is afraid of repercussions in Iran.
Near the shrine, Mohammad Yasin Ahmadi, 15, has come from the Iranian city of Qom on his second pilgrimage. He says many Iranians came this year because of Ayatollah Khamenei, who visited Iraq in the 1950s but was never able to come as Iran's supreme leader.
Before Khamenei was buried in July in his hometown in Iran, his body was brought to the Iraqi holy cities of Karbala and Najaf.
"Most people came for him this year," Ahmadi says. "This Arbaeen has the scent and the feeling of the Ayatollah."
